Irreversible operations ¶ These operations can make a chip unusable for good A locked chip, a required channel whose keys you lost, an I2C address your board does not use, a deleted module: none of them comes back. A chip is cheap; the product it is soldered into is not. Run each operation on a spare chip first, keep the keys it depends on in two places, and write down what you did. Datasheet sections this page relies on SetLockState, DisableObjectCreation, SetPlatformSCPRequest: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Module management commands, p. 73 SetAppletFeatures, TriggerSelfTest, ReadState: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Module management commands, p. 76 DeleteAll: factory reset role, unwrapped reply: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, DeleteAll, p. 154 PERSO applet needs no authentication: anyone can change the address: NXP AN13015 Rev. 1.4, Deleting the PERSO applet, p. 19 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The flow ¶ Irreversible operations: plan, confirm, apply Figure description and sources Left to right. The build must define SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE, or none of these calls exists. The caller asks irreversible::Operations for a Plan of one operation: the Plan sends nothing, checks the arguments, the capabilities and the role, and says what will change. The caller shows the Plan to a person and builds a Confirmation of the same operation from its phrase. Apply() takes both; a Plan of another operation, a phrase of another operation or a Plan that was not prepared is refused before any byte is sent (Error::IrreversibleNotConfirmed). The operation tags are read from inc/se05x_confirm.hpp; the two PERSO operations live on perso::Perso and follow the same flow. Drawn from: inc/se05x_confirm.hpp operation tags ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/irreversible-flow.py . Build flag. The calls exist only when the build defines SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE (CMake option or Kconfig; off by default). A production build that never needs them never contains them. Plan. irreversible::Operations

::Plan...() checks the device state, the arguments, the chip's capabilities, the role the command needs ( ConditionsNotSatisfied ) and that the chip is not already in the requested state ( WrongState ), sends nothing, and returns a Plan with the target, a one-line Effect() for the operator and the arguments it will send. Confirmation. A person reads the plan and types the operation's phrase; the code builds Confirmation{typed} from what the person typed, never from Op::kPhrase itself. A phrase of another operation gives a confirmation that is not confirmed. Apply. Apply(plan, confirmation) is the only call that sends. A plan that was not prepared, a plan prepared for another device, or a confirmation that does not match, is refused with IrreversibleNotConfirmed before any byte goes on the bus; the state, gate and role are checked again. /// Lock the transport for good. Run it from a session with the Transport credential; show the /// plan's effect to a person; the phrase is typed by that person, not by the code that planned it. template < se05x :: PortSet P > se05x :: Error LockForGood ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , const se05x :: irreversible :: Phrase & typed , void ( * show )( const char * effect )) noexcept { using Op = se05x :: irreversible :: SetLockStatePersistent ; se05x :: irreversible :: Operations < P > operations ( device ); const auto plan = operations . PlanSetLockStatePersistent (); // sends nothing if ( ! plan . ok ()) { return plan . error ; // ConditionsNotSatisfied: not a Transport session; WrongState: locked } show ( plan . value . Effect ()); return operations . Apply ( plan . value , se05x :: irreversible :: Confirmation < Op > { typed }). error ; } The snippet is compiled with the flag on and run against the chip model ( tests/test_irreversible.cpp ). A confirmation is a type per operation: passing a Confirmation for a DeleteAllObjects plan does not compile. hrot:: never offers these operations. TriggerSelfTest is not irreversible but resets the chip without a reply, so it takes an irreversible::ResetExpected acknowledgement instead. The operations ¶ Operation What it does Role or precondition Undo SetLockStatePersistent Persistent transport lock: only five commands answered Transport session Only from a Transport session; lost key: never RequirePlatformScp Every command needs full platform SCP03 from then on PlatformScp session Only over platform SCP03 ( AllowWithoutPlatformSCP ); lost keys: never ReplacePlatformKeys Replaces the platform SCP03 key set. Not available : the plan returns Unsupported , sends nothing ( Secure channels ) Platform SCP03 open Only with the new keys ChangeAppletFeatures Changes the AppletConfig and feature bits Feature session (NXP-owned credential) Depends on the chip; features may not come back DeleteAllObjects Deletes every object except provisioned ones; the reply is not wrapped (AN12543 4.20.5, p. 154), so its success is not authenticated: check afterwards, for example that a known object is gone; the session ends and the device selects the applet again FactoryReset session Never: the keys are gone DisableObjectCreation No new objects (or none at all) Restrict session Persistent form: never CreateImmutableObject A binary object of 1 to 512 bytes written once; the plan refuses a policy that grants Write or Delete to anyone (that object is not irreversible: use WriteBinary ) Its policy Never CreateFiniteAuthObject A UserID authentication object with 1 to 255 attempts; the plan checks the value length of the generation Its policy The object locks when the counter runs out ChangeI2cAddress New 7-bit address after the next reset. Not available : no applet command (A7); the plan returns Unsupported SE051 PERSO Only by a host that uses the new address ApplyAppletUpdate SEMS Lite applet update. Not available in this version: the plan returns Unsupported Out of v1 Anti-rollback: never back ReplaceEcKeyCredential Replaces the ECKey session credential. Not available : the update of an authentication object's key is not described in the sources read; the plan returns Unsupported Feature or user session Only with the new credential WritePersoSetting PERSO tag write (address, I2C parameters, ATR and CIP bytes) on perso::Perso SE051, PERSO selectable A wrong flavour leaves the chip silent to this host DeletePersoModule Deletes iot_extended or rsakeygen on perso::Perso SE051 A and C Never; iot_base is never offered The two creating operations are the only way to make those objects: outside a plan the device refuses, before sending, a WriteBinary that would create a file whose policy grants neither Write nor Delete ( policy::IsImmutable ) and every WriteUserId (each UserID object has a finite counter and locks for good when it runs out), both with IrreversibleNotConfirmed . The facade's own keys and counters are permanent too (their policies forbid delete); that is the facade's documented contract, not one of these operations: plan the slots before you provision ( Getting started ). Device::ExecuteIrreversible checks, before it sends anything: the confirmation ( IrreversibleNotConfirmed ), the state and the gate as Execute does, the session role of the table ( ConditionsNotSatisfied ), and that the chip is not already in the requested state ( WrongState for a persistent lock that is set or platform SCP03 that is already required). Sources: SetLockState, DisableObjectCreation and SetPlatformSCPRequest AN12543 pp. 73-76; DeleteAll p. 154; PERSO AN13015 pp. 19 and 49; the session preconditions AN13030 pp. 679-682. Before you apply ¶ Read the chip with ReadState and GetVersion() and keep the output. Check you hold the keys of every role the result will need: the Transport key after a lock, the platform keys after requiring SCP03. On an SE051, check the PERSO applet is still selectable before a PERSO write and that your host build speaks the flavour you are about to select. Never run an irreversible operation in a loop or on a schedule. Keep the bytes behind a plan's ByteSpan (the data of an immutable object, the value of a UserID object) unchanged until Apply() : a plan copies the arguments, never a secret.

docs.text: Choose your job ¶ The SE050, SE051 and SE052 are secure elements: a small chip on the I2C bus that holds keys and secrets your firmware uses but can never read out, and that signs, agrees keys, counts and attests on its behalf (SE050 data sheet section 3, p. 6; AN12543 section 3, pp. 6-47). Pick what you want the chip to do; each guide has a diagram, compiled code, what it protects against, what to do when a call fails, and a bench step. What the chip does for your firmware Figure description and sources Your firmware connects to the SE05x over I2C, T=1, SCP03. From the SE05x nine jobs follow. Root of trust is a device identity key that never leaves the chip. Secret storage holds a Wi-Fi passphrase, tokens and configuration. Certificates and signing covers CSR, chain and ECDSA. TLS and mutual-auth gives client credentials. Key agreement is ECDH with a peer. Secure sessions make the bus encrypted and authenticated. Attestation is a signed answer, checked on the host. Monotonic counters hold anti-rollback floors. Secure provisioning and lifecycle locks set up and lock a device. Drawn from: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml . You want to Guide Driver API Keep a Wi-Fi passphrase, a cloud token or a configuration in the chip, read only over an encrypted channel Store a secret hrot::Device::Store , Load with Protection::Secret Give the device an identity key and sign with it Device identity Provision<KeyUse::Sign> , Sign , VerifySignature Get a certificate for that key and keep the chain CSR and certificates pki::BuildCsr , pki::StoreCertificate , pki::VerifyChain Authenticate to a server with TLS client credentials Mutual TLS Provision<KeyUse::TlsClient> , TlsSign Agree a key with a peer and encrypt with it ECDH Provision<KeyUse::Agree> , Agree Make the bus itself encrypted and authenticated Secure channel Device::SetPlatformKeys , Open , BeginAesKeySession Refuse firmware older than what already ran Anti-rollback CreateCounter , CheckFloor , RaiseCounterTo Check on the host that a key lives in a chip holding an attestation key you trust Attested reads Attest , TrustAttestationKey Set up a device in the factory and lock what must not change Provisioning irreversible::Operations New to the chip? Start with the first 15 minutes , then pick the variant on Where to use it . The threats each job answers are on the Security model . What every job assumes ¶ The bus can be probed. Open the chip with platform SCP03 at Full (or an AESKey session); the facade refuses a key, counter or secret call over a bus whose answers are not authenticated, and sends nothing ( PolicyDenied ). Until RequirePlatformScp has been applied the chip also takes plain commands from anyone on the bus: provision in a trusted place and apply it before the device leaves ( Security model ). The chip runs applet 7.x. The facade runs on the SE050E, SE051 and SE052. On applet 3.x (SE050 A to D and F) and 6.x (SE051 on early boards) every facade call returns Unsupported and sends nothing once its argument checks pass (an invalid key, an off-curve point or an empty buffer is refused first with InvalidArgument ); use se05x::Device there ( Choosing a variant ). Slots are planned. A facade key or counter can never be deleted; only a factory reset removes it. Plan the slots before the first Provision ( Getting started by job ). Nothing here is verified on hardware yet. Every guide gives the bench step that confirms it on a dev kit.

docs.text: Lifecycle and roles ¶ The chip-wide settings of the IoT applet, the command that changes each one, and the reserved authentication object whose session the chip demands for it. Datasheet sections this page relies on Reserved object identifiers: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Table 5, p. 10 SetLockState, DisableObjectCreation, SetPlatformSCPRequest: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Module management commands, p. 73 SetAppletFeatures, TriggerSelfTest, ReadState: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Module management commands, p. 76 DeleteSecureObject; provisioned objects stay: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, DeleteSecureObject, p. 96 DeleteAll: factory reset role, unwrapped reply: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, DeleteAll, p. 154 Lifecycle commands and their session preconditions: NXP AN13030 Rev. 2.7, SetLockState, SetPlatformSCPRequest, SetAppletFeatures, p. 679 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Lifecycle settings and the roles that change them Figure description and sources The device-wide settings of the IoT applet, each changed by one command that the chip accepts only in a session opened with one reserved authentication object (the AuthRole of inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp, checked by RequiredRole() before anything is sent). Transport lock: SetLockState from a Transport session; while locked the chip answers only GetVersion, ReadState, the read of the unique id, GetRandom and CreateSession (AN12543 Table 19); the persistent lock survives resets and is lifted only from a Transport session again. Platform SCP required: SetPlatformSCPRequest from a PlatformScp session; from then on every command needs full platform SCP03. Restricted object creation: DisableObjectCreation; the persistent form cannot be undone. Applet features: SetAppletFeatures from a Feature (ECKey) session. docs.text: Limitations ¶ What the driver does not do, what it holds back, and what has not been checked. Each item says why. Datasheet sections this page relies on From NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5: APDU buffer 270 bytes, internal buffer 1024 bytes: APDU buffer sizes, p. 3 ImportExternalObject: ImportExternalObject, p. 88 AEAD one-shot limit 888 bytes: AEADOneShot, p. 125 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Not supported ¶ Item Why ISO 7816 and ISO 14443 interfaces A host cannot reach them over I2C; they are chip-side interfaces SE051P It runs a customer applet and has no IoT applet T4T applet (SE051H NFC file system) A separate applet, not in AN12543 SEMS Lite applet update agent Its applet interface document is not published; the raw GlobalPlatform channel stays SCP02, SCP11 Not offered by the chip in the public documents X.509 parsing in the facade The facade stores and reads certificate bytes; DER, CSR and X.509 are the optional se05x::pki layer Platform key replacement, I2C address change, applet update, ECKey credential replacement The irreversible plans return Unsupported ( Irreversible operations ) The HRoT facade on applet 3.x (SE050 A to D, F) and 6.x (SE051 on early boards) Every facade call returns Unsupported before anything is sent, after its argument checks (an invalid key, an off-curve point or an empty buffer is refused first with InvalidArgument ); the device layer ( se05x::Device ) serves these chips Reading with Load or Attest a data object that Store did not write Store ends every object with a completion marker (0xA5). An object without it (written by Device or another tool) is FrameError ; one that happens to end in 0xA5 reads back one byte short. Read such objects with Device::ReadObject Facade curves other than NIST P-256 The facade keys are P-256 (every variant has it, and the crypto port verifies it); other curves through Device TPM 2.0 A host-side software stack over the vendor middleware, not a chip command set ImportExternalObject The vendor asks to be contacted before use (AN12543 p. 88) Held until confirmed ¶ The ECKey session key derivation is written from AN12543 but has no test vector: built behind a flag. The NXP-flavour CRC byte order is not in UM11225: both orders are tried in Auto . The length form of the TLVs in an attested answer is not fixed by the documents: the signature is checked over the bytes as returned (A21). Which NAD and MPOT unit a chip uses in the GP flavour, and whether Auto reaches every variant (A17, A32). Whether platform SCP03 in the default session satisfies a policy's REQUIRE_SM, and that facade objects made in one applet session are refused in another (A20). The SE050 boot time before the first frame is not in the documents: Config::boot_wait_ms (20 ms) then polling. The policy bit values of applet 6.x are not in any obtained document. Irreversible operations are compiled out by default. The length form an attestation hashes under secure messaging ( Ambiguities ). DeleteAll is sent with the Lc 0x00 byte of AN12543 Table 339; the vendor middleware sends four bytes. Both should be accepted; a trace of a real chip decides it ( Ambiguities ). Limits of the chip the driver enforces ¶ The applet's APDU buffer is 270 bytes and its internal buffer 1024 (AN12543 p. 3); an AEAD one-shot carries at most 888 bytes (p. 125); EdDSA sign and verify at most 940 bytes of input, 919 inside a UserID session (pp. 103-104); an attested binary read at most 500 bytes per chunk; one applet session at a time through Device (the chip allows two); the throughput limit of SW 0x66A6 ( Errors and status words ). TLSPerformPRF takes the host's TLS role ( TlsPrfArgs::role ) to choose which random it passes (AN12543 4.17.3). Not verified ¶ Nothing has run on hardware. Every transport, timing and secure-channel behaviour is from the documents, the vendor middleware as a test oracle and an independent chip model. Bench steps are on every row of Ambiguities . No trace of a real chip is in the test vectors yet. The certification of the chip (FIPS 140-2 on the SE050F, FIPS 140-3 on the SE052F) covers the chip, not this driver. See also Ambiguities for every open question and its knob.

docs.text: Mechanization policy ¶ Where each defect class of the catalogue is caught, and how a class moves to a cheaper catch. The goal: a defect is found by the cheapest check that can find it, and reviewers spend their time on judgement, not on what a script can do. Decision rule ¶ Catch a class at the first level that can decide it without judgement, in order of cost: Lint ( tools/preflight.sh , runs in seconds, on every builder's machine). Use it when the defect is a pattern in text or syntax: a forbidden include, a MISRA rule CodeQL reports, a missing else , a parameter name, a symbol named in docs that does not exist, a missing gitlink. Test, model or mutation (host tests, the chip model's fault knobs, fuzz properties, compile-fail cases, mutants of a fix). Use it when the defect is behaviour: what the driver sends or returns when the chip or the bus misbehaves. A test is the right level when the model can be made to misbehave in exactly that way. Independent review question (a reviewer who did not write the code). Use it only for what needs judgement: whether the datasheet was read correctly, whether a state machine is complete, whether the model is independent of the driver, whether a doc claim is true. Every catalogue entry names its level under DETECTION. A class with no lint or test is a review class and costs reviewer time every round; it is a candidate for promotion. Promotion ¶ A defect that reached a reviewer or the CI of a second driver is promoted one level up: review to test, test to lint where a pattern exists. The reviewer who finds the second occurrence writes the promotion item in the round's report; the template maintainer (the agent or person that owns the template branch) implements it before the next driver's first push, or records why it cannot be mechanised in the catalogue entry. A defect that reached a third driver after its promotion means the check is wrong: fix the check first, then look at the driver. Demotion never happens by silence: a check is removed only with a catalogue note saying what replaced it. What a lint may and may not do ¶ It reports file:line , the catalogue id, and the fix. It exits non-zero on a finding, in the preflight and the gate. It has no false-positive tolerance : before merging, it runs over every finished driver and the template; any finding on a driver that CI shows clean is a false positive, and the lint is not merged until it has none (narrow the pattern; do not add an ignore list per driver). It may be conservative the other way (miss cases): then the catalogue says partial and names the review question that covers the rest. It never edits files, never skips silently (a missing tool is reported as a skipped step in the final line, and the gate treats a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step as a failure), and has a selftest with one bad and one good case. It does not replace the CI scan: CI is the final word for MISRA. Recording a new finding ¶ Append the finding to its catalogue entry (driver, review round or CI report file, finding id) and update the count and the index table; add a new entry only when no class fits. Write the check at the level the rules above give: the lint, or the test pattern (model knob, mutant, fuzz property), or the reviewer's question in the skill. Run it over the finished drivers (lint) or add the regression test that fails without the fix (test). Add a CHANGELOG.md entry under [Unreleased] and the template change is released as a new template commit; drivers take it with scaffold.py --check-drift --fix (the skills and tools are managed files), which updates the template pin in .kokeb/template.yml . Mention the catalogue id in the commit subject. The pre-push gate ¶ A driver is cleared for its first push only by kokeb-tools/gate.sh <chip> (the orchestrator's script, one run per driver through the shared Docker lock). It writes a log and a verdict, and PASS needs all of: container preflight ( tools/preflight.sh --container ) with 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) , including the MISRA scan and the ESP32 builds; a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step is a FAIL; handbook_check reports 0 errors (this includes the library-subset include scan); tools/check_standalone.py passes; template drift: scaffold.py --check-drift reports nothing; no .pdf file is tracked; the examples/esp32/scripts gitlink (mode 160000) is present; the tree is staged as it will be committed. No silent skips: every step prints a line, and a missing tool fails the gate. Roles ¶ Builders write code, models, tests and docs and run host tests and the quick preflight. They do not run the container gate, push, or create repositories. The gate runner is one serialized worker that runs gate.sh for one driver at a time and reports the verdict and the log; it does not edit the driver. Reviewers are read-only and independent. They are given the code, the model, the datasheet, the catalogue and the previous round's report, and never the builder's conclusions (the build report is read only in the claims-vs-code step). They run the review-round protocol. Fixers change the driver, fix at the cause, add the test that fails without the fix, and answer each finding id. The template maintainer applies promotions and keeps the catalogue current. Backlog of promotions (state of the catalogue) ¶ The classes whose target level is above their present level are listed in the catalogue index: RD-12 to RD-18 and RD-23 (MISRA patterns, one misra_lint with a rule per id), RD-20 and RD-22 (ESP-IDF and compile-fail lints), RD-08 ( claims-symbols ), RD-07 (model standalone lint), RD-06, RD-01, RD-02, RD-03, RD-05, RD-10 and RD-25 (shared model knobs and a template mutation runner), RD-21 (host start-up test of the ESP32 port).

docs.text: Objects and policies ¶ Everything the chip keeps is a secure object with an identifier, a class and a policy set. The chip checks the policy on every command; the host never decides access. Datasheet sections this page relies on APDU buffer 270 bytes, internal buffer 1024 bytes: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, APDU buffer sizes, p. 3 Reserved object identifiers: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Table 5, p. 10 Authentication object 0 is the default session only: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, 3.7.1.2 Policy, p. 36 Session policy and object policy headers: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Tables 62 and 63, p. 66 WriteBinary, WriteUserID, WriteCounter: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, WriteBinary, WriteUserID, WriteCounter, p. 84 DeleteSecureObject; provisioned objects stay: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, DeleteSecureObject, p. 96 Pre-provisioned attestation keys: NXP AN12436 Rev. 2.4, Tables 8 and 9, p. 10 Object identifier ranges: NXP AN13904 Rev. 1.0, Object identifier ranges, p. 7 Policy flag layouts per applet generation: NXP AN13030 Rev. 2.7, Policy table for 3.x, 6.x and 7.x, p. 53 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Objects, policies and sessions Figure description and sources Every key or data item on the chip is a secure object: a 4-byte identifier, a class (ObjectClass of inc/se05x_ids.hpp), a lifetime (persistent, or transient: the content is lost at reset or deselect) and an origin (generated inside, written from outside, or provisioned by the vendor; attestation reports it). At creation the object gets a policy set: each policy names one authentication object and the operations it may do (the Rule enumeration of inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp, 9 to 53 bytes per policy; AN12543 Table 63). An authentication object is itself a secure object (a UserID, an AES key or an EC key); a session opened with it (at most 2 at a time) is what a policy checks. The policy builder only builds rules valid for the class and generation, and the facade uses the strict profile only. Drawn from: inc/se05x_ids.hpp ObjectClass, Origin, Lifetime ; inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp Rule ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/object-policy.py . Identifiers ¶ An ObjectId is 4 bytes, big endian on the wire. The ranges (AN13904 p. 7, AN12543 Table 5): Range Owner The driver 0x00000000 to 0x7BFFFFFF Your objects MakeUserObject() accepts them 0x7C000000 to 0x7DFFFFFF Android key master, demos refused for writes 0x7FFF0000 to 0x7FFFFFFF The applet's reserved objects ReservedId ; never written 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF The vendor (provisioned keys and certificates) read only Reserved objects the driver names include the transport lock ( 0x7FFF0200 ), the ECKey session key ( 0x7FFF0201 ), external import ( 0x7FFF0202 ), feature ( 0x7FFF0204 ), factory reset ( 0x7FFF0205 ), unique id ( 0x7FFF0206 ), platform SCP ( 0x7FFF0207 ), I2C controller access ( 0x7FFF0208 ) and restrict ( 0x7FFF020A ). Classes, lifetime and origin ¶ Keys (EC, RSA, AES, DES, HMAC), binary files, UserIDs, counters and PCRs. A transient object keeps its descriptor in flash and its content in RAM: the content is lost at reset or deselect. Every object records its origin (generated inside, written from outside, provisioned by the vendor), and an attestation reports it. Policies ¶ A policy set is a list of policies. Each names one authentication object and a 4-byte header of allowed operations. Authentication object 0 ( PolicyBuilder::ForAllOthers() ) is the default session only, the one without an applet session: an AESKey, ECKey or UserID session does not inherit it (AN12543 3.7.1.2, p. 36), so a policy meant for a session names its credential with For() ( Ambiguities , A20). Some rules carry extensions; one policy is 9 to 53 bytes (AN12543 Table 63, pp. 66-67). Rules include sign, verify, key agreement, encrypt, decrypt, KDF, unwrap, read, write, generate, delete, require secure messaging, require a PCR value, attestation, import and export, and forbid derived output. The rules differ by applet generation (AN13030 p. 53): 7.x adds read and write to the common rules and moves several symmetric-key rules. PolicyBuilder<Generation, Class> builds only the rules valid for the class and the generation; a rule that does not exist there does not compile. The facade builds with the strict profile only: no private-key read, no write or delete by others, secure messaging where the bus is exposed. The open profile needs a named reason. Sizes ¶ The applet's APDU buffer is 270 bytes and its internal buffer 1024 (AN12543 p. 3). An AEAD one-shot carries at most 888 bytes, a binary object up to 0x7FFF bytes, a counter 1 to 8 bytes. FreeMemory() reports 2 bytes on the SE050 and SE051 (0x7FFF means at least 32768) and 4 bytes on the SE052 (AN12543 p. 153). Deleting ¶ DeleteSecureObject needs the delete rule; a provisioned object cannot be deleted (AN12543 p. 96). DeleteAll is a lifecycle operation ( Lifecycle ).

docs.text: Certificates (PKI) ¶ se05x::pki is an optional layer for the device side of a public key infrastructure: it asks for a certificate for a key that lives in the chip, stores the certificate the CA issues so nobody can change it, and checks a certificate chain up to a trust anchor you choose. It allocates nothing, throws nothing, and works only in buffers you pass in. It is opt-in: #include "se05x_pki.hpp" . The umbrella header se05x.hpp does not include it, and nothing else in the driver depends on it. Device certificates: provision once, verify at boot Figure description and sources Left to right, top row once in the factory, bottom row at every boot. 1. The chip generates the key pair; only the public key comes out (ReadPublicKey). 2. BuildCsr writes the request and the chip signs its digest (DeviceSigner); VerifyCsr checks it against its own key. 3. The CA, outside the driver, issues the certificate. 4. StoreCertificate writes the certificate and the CA certificate (the trust anchor) into new binary objects with read-only policies, in one WriteBinary each, and reads them back. At boot: ReadCertificate and LoadTrustAnchor read them, VerifyChain checks signature, names, time, constraints and path length with the caller's clock, and the verified key is the chip's own. The CA, revocation and TLS are outside the driver. Drawn from: inc/se05x_pki_csr.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_device.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_verify.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/pki-provisioning.py . What it does and what it does not do ¶ It does It does not Write and read DER strictly ( der::Writer , der::Reader ) Accept BER: indefinite lengths, long forms for short lengths, multi-byte tags Build PKCS#10 requests (RFC 2986) signed by a chip key ( DeviceSigner ) or a crypto-port key ( PortSigner ) Generate or hold a private key on the host Parse X.509 v3 certificates with ECDSA P-256 / P-384 keys and Ed25519 keys Parse RSA, other curves, v1 or v2 certificates Verify a chain to your trust anchors: signatures, names, time, basic constraints, key usage, path length Check revocation (CRL, OCSP), certificate policies, name constraints or extended key usage Store certificates and trust anchors in binary objects with read-only policies, and read them back Act as a CA, run a TLS stack, or talk to a cloud service Anything outside the profile is refused with a reason, never skipped: an unknown critical extension, a GeneralizedTime before 2050, a duplicate extension, a parameter where RFC 5758 says none, a compressed point. Provisioning recipe ¶ The four steps below are compiled for a board and run against the chip model in the tests ( tests/docs/pki_recipes.hpp , tests/test_pki_recipes.cpp ). Run them with platform SCP03 open ( HRoT cookbook ): the key policy requires secure messaging. 1. Generate the key in the chip ¶ /// Step 1: generate the device key inside the chip and read its public half. The policy lets /// anybody sign with it under secure messaging and nobody write, delete or regenerate it. template < AppletGeneration G , PortSet P > Result < pki :: PublicKey > GenerateDeviceKey ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , ObjectId key , std :: span < uint8_t , 65 > public_key ) noexcept { const Result < Policy > policy = PolicyBuilder < G , ObjectClass :: EcKeyPair , Profile :: Strict > {} . ForAllOthers () . template Allow < Rule :: Sign > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Write > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Delete > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Gen > () . RequireSecureMessaging () . Build (); if ( ! policy . ok ()) { return Result < pki :: PublicKey >:: Failure ( policy . error , policy . detail ); } if ( const auto made = device . GenerateEcKey ( key , policy . value , EcCurve :: NistP256 ); ! made . ok ()) { return Result < pki :: PublicKey >:: Failure ( made . error , made . detail ); } return pki :: ReadPublicKey ( device , key , pki :: KeyType :: EcP256 , MutableByteSpan { public_key }); } 2. Ask for a certificate ¶ The chip signs the SHA-256 digest of the request info. VerifyCsr() then checks the request with the public key in it: a key id that does not belong to that public key is caught here, before the request reaches a CA. /// Step 2: a certification request for that key, signed by the chip, with the chip's unique id /// as the subject's serialNumber. The request is checked against its own key before it leaves. template < PortSet P , typename Crypto > Result < std :: size_t > MakeCsr ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , Crypto & crypto , ObjectId key , const pki :: PublicKey & public_key , ByteSpan unique_id , MutableByteSpan csr ) noexcept { constexpr std :: array < uint8_t , 6 > kOrganization { 0x44U , 0x65U , 0x76U , 0x69U , 0x63U , 0x65U }; pki :: Name subject {}; static_cast < void > ( subject . Add ( pki :: Attribute :: Organization , ByteSpan { kOrganization }) . AddHex ( pki :: Attribute :: SerialNumber , unique_id )); const pki :: CsrRequest request { & subject , public_key , nullptr , pki :: key_usage :: kDigitalSignature }; pki :: DeviceSigner < P > signer ( device , key , pki :: KeyType :: EcP256 ); const Result < std :: size_t > built = pki :: BuildCsr ( request , signer , crypto , csr ); if ( ! built . ok ()) { return built ; } pki :: PortVerifier < Crypto > verifier ( crypto ); const auto checked = pki :: VerifyCsr ( ByteSpan { csr }. first ( built . value ), verifier , crypto ); return checked . ok () ? built : Result < std :: size_t >:: Failure ( checked . error , checked . detail ); } Text values are UTF-8 bytes: the layer never converts characters. Name::AddHex() writes bytes (the chip's unique id) as upper-case hex. countryName and serialNumber are PrintableString (X.520), every other attribute UTF8String (RFC 5280 4.1.2.6). Ask for a subjectAltName with AltNames (DNS name, URI, e-mail, IP address). 3. Store the certificate and the trust anchor ¶ /// Step 3: store the certificate the CA issued, and the CA's certificate as the trust anchor, /// each in a new binary object nobody can write; `admin` may delete them to rotate. template < AppletGeneration G , PortSet P > Result < void > ImportCertificates ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , ObjectId certificate , ByteSpan issued , ObjectId anchor , ByteSpan ca_certificate , AuthObject admin ) noexcept { const Result < Policy > policy = pki :: CertificatePolicy < G > ( admin ); if ( ! policy . ok ()) { return Result < void >:: Failure ( policy . error , policy . detail ); } std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > scratch {}; const auto stored_anchor = pki :: StoreCertificate ( device , anchor , ca_certificate , policy . value , scratch ); if ( ! stored_anchor . ok ()) { return stored_anchor ; } return pki :: StoreCertificate ( device , certificate , issued , policy . value , scratch ); } StoreCertificate() follows four rules, and refuses before sending anything when one fails: the certificate must parse; the policy must not grant Write to anyone, nor Delete to everybody ( PolicyAllowsWrite ): a policy is fixed when the object is created, so a read-only policy locks the content; the certificate must fit one WriteBinary command, because a read-only object cannot take a second write: at most MaxStoredCertificate(policy) bytes, 999 with CertificatePolicy() and 990 with an administrator ( ObjectTooLarge ); an existing object is never overwritten ( ObjectExists ). It then reads the object back and compares it ( ReadBackMismatch ). To rotate a certificate, give CertificatePolicy() an administrator: that session may delete the object, and a new one is stored. 4. Check the chain at every boot ¶ /// At every boot: read the certificate and the anchor back and verify the chain at `now` (Unix /// seconds from a clock you trust). The verified key is the one the chip signs with. template < PortSet P , typename Crypto > Error CheckDeviceCertificate ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , Crypto & crypto , ObjectId certificate , ObjectId anchor , uint64_t now ) noexcept { std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > anchor_bytes {}; std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > cert_bytes {}; const auto trusted = pki :: LoadTrustAnchor ( device , anchor , anchor_bytes ); const auto cert = pki :: ReadCertificate ( device , certificate , cert_bytes ); if ( ! trusted . ok () || ! cert . ok ()) { return trusted . ok () ? cert . error : trusted . error ; } const std :: array < ByteSpan , 1 > chain { cert . value . der }; const std :: array < pki :: TrustAnchor , 1 > anchors { trusted . value }; pki :: PortVerifier < Crypto > verifier ( crypto ); const pki :: VerifyOptions options { now , pki :: key_usage :: kDigitalSignature , false }; const auto verified = pki :: VerifyChain ( std :: span < const ByteSpan > { chain }, std :: span < const pki :: TrustAnchor > { anchors }, options , verifier , crypto ); return verified . error ; // AttestationInvalid: pki::ReasonOf(verified.detail) says why } The time is yours: Unix seconds from a clock you trust. A time of 0 is refused ( NoTime ); the check is never skipped. A device that has no trustworthy time yet must get one first: a wrong clock makes an expired certificate look valid. Chain verification ¶ VerifyChain(chain, anchors, options, verifier, hasher) takes the chain end entity first, without the anchor, at most kMaxChain (6) certificates, and up to kMaxAnchors (8) anchors. From the anchor down it checks (RFC 5280 6.1): Check Reason when it fails Each certificate parses under the profile the parser's reason The issuer is the subject above, byte for byte NameMismatch The signature verifies with the key above; P-256 with ecdsa-with-SHA256, P-384 with ecdsa-with-SHA384 SignatureInvalid , AlgorithmMismatch now is within notBefore and notAfter, both included NotYetValid , Expired Every issuing certificate has cA TRUE, and keyCertSign when it has a keyUsage NotCa , KeyCertSignMissing No more intermediates than any pathLenConstraint above (and the anchor's) allows PathLengthExceeded The end entity has options.required_key_usage and is no CA unless allow_ca_leaf LeafKeyUsageMissing , LeafIsCa Every intermediate counts toward the path length, self-issued or not: stricter than RFC 5280 6.1.4 (l). Names are compared byte for byte, which a chain from one CA meets; a CA that re-encodes names is refused ( NameMismatch ). The verifier is a port: SignatureVerifier verifies a fixed-width r || s over a digest. PortVerifier<C> adapts any crypto port and verifies P-256 (the port's EcdsaP256Verify ); a P-384 chain needs a verifier that supports P-384, or it is refused ( CurveNotSupported ). The digest comes from the crypto port's Hash . Ed25519 signatures are not verified by this layer ( UnsupportedAlgorithm ). Errors ¶ Every call returns a Result . When the PKI layer refuses, Detail::layer is Layer::Pki and pki::ReasonOf(detail) names the rule; pki::ToString(reason) gives its name. The coarse Error is: Error Reasons InvalidArgument malformed DER, a field outside the profile, a bad builder argument, NoTime Unsupported a version, algorithm, curve or critical extension the layer does not handle; CurveNotSupported AttestationInvalid a chain check failed: NameMismatch to LeafIsCa BufferTooSmall BufferTooSmall , ObjectTooLarge CryptoFailure the crypto port or a signer failed A failure of the device (the bus, a status word, the capability gate) keeps the device's own Error and Detail . Keys and algorithms ¶ Key Request (CSR) Certificate parse Chain verify P-256 chip ( DeviceSigner ) or crypto port ( PortSigner ) yes PortVerifier or your verifier P-384 chip yes your verifier Ed25519 chip, EdDSASign over the request (not on SE052F; at most 940 bytes, 919 in a UserID session: AN12543 pp. 103-104) yes (key) no Limits ¶ Limit Value Nesting depth of the reader and writer der::kMaxDepth = 10 Length of one DER element der::kMaxLength = 65535 bytes Certificates in a chain, anchors per call 6, 8 Name attributes, alternative names in a request 8, 8 Extensions of one certificate 16 Stored certificate MaxStoredCertificate(policy) Not verified on hardware ¶ The chip model of the tests stores binary objects and P-256 keys only. On a real chip, still to be run on a bench: P-384: GenerateEcKey(id, policy, EcCurve::NistP384) , ReadPublicKey(..., KeyType::EcP384, ...) returns 97 bytes, a DeviceSigner request verifies with openssl req -verify . Ed25519: the same with EcCurve::Ed25519 and KeyType::Ed25519 on SE050E or SE051; check that the public key read back and reversed (AN12543 7.1) is the one in the request, and openssl req -verify accepts it. A certificate of about 990 bytes stored with CertificatePolicy() reads back equal; a write to it is refused by the chip ( PolicyDenied ). How it is tested ¶ The vectors in tests/vectors/pki_vectors.hpp were made with OpenSSL from keys generated for that run and deleted; the requests use the published RFC 6979 and RFC 8032 test keys. The tests compare the request info byte for byte with OpenSSL's, build the Ed25519 request byte for byte, verify OpenSSL's chains, and check every refusal on an edited copy of a vector. Two libFuzzer targets ( fuzz_pki_der , fuzz_pki_x509 ) check that the reader re-encodes every element it accepts to the same bytes and that the parser and the chain walk never accept what they should refuse. Each guard has a one-edit mutant in tools/mutants/pki.txt that the tests kill.

docs.text: Every call returns a Result . When the PKI layer refuses, Detail::layer is Layer::Pki and pki::ReasonOf(detail) names the rule; pki::ToString(reason) gives its name. The coarse Error is: Error Reasons InvalidArgument malformed DER, a field outside the profile, a bad builder argument, NoTime Unsupported a version, algorithm, curve or critical extension the layer does not handle; CurveNotSupported AttestationInvalid a chain check failed: NameMismatch to LeafIsCa BufferTooSmall BufferTooSmall , ObjectTooLarge CryptoFailure the crypto port or a signer failed A failure of the device (the bus, a status word, the capability gate) keeps the device's own Error and Detail .

docs.text: The chip model of the tests stores binary objects and P-256 keys only. On a real chip, still to be run on a bench: P-384: GenerateEcKey(id, policy, EcCurve::NistP384) , ReadPublicKey(..., KeyType::EcP384, ...) returns 97 bytes, a DeviceSigner request verifies with openssl req -verify . Ed25519: the same with EcCurve::Ed25519 and KeyType::Ed25519 on SE050E or SE051; check that the public key read back and reversed (AN12543 7.1) is the one in the request, and openssl req -verify accepts it. A certificate of about 990 bytes stored with CertificatePolicy() reads back equal; a write to it is refused by the chip ( PolicyDenied ).
docs.title: Not verified on hardware

docs.text: The vectors in tests/vectors/pki_vectors.hpp were made with OpenSSL from keys generated for that run and deleted; the requests use the published RFC 6979 and RFC 8032 test keys. The tests compare the request info byte for byte with OpenSSL's, build the Ed25519 request byte for byte, verify OpenSSL's chains, and check every refusal on an edited copy of a vector. Two libFuzzer targets ( fuzz_pki_der , fuzz_pki_x509 ) check that the reader re-encodes every element it accepts to the same bytes and that the parser and the chain walk never accept what they should refuse. Each guard has a one-edit mutant in tools/mutants/pki.txt that the tests kill.

Piece Where What it is Port examples/<platform>/ The classes that implement the bus, clock and optional reset hooks for that MCU or OS ( Porting ) Example examples/<platform>/ A program that runs the driver there, built by CI Build integration the root CMakeLists.txt How that platform's build system finds the driver What exists today ¶ Platform Port Example Build integration Built by CI Host (Linux, macOS, Windows) the chip model of the tests ( tests/model/ ) and tests/null_ports.hpp (a bus with nothing on it) examples/host/ Plain CMake yes ESP32 (ESP-IDF) examples/esp32/main/esp32_se05x_port.hpp examples/esp32/ (built with ESP-IDF v5.5; not run on a board) Component yes STM32, RP2040, nRF, other MCUs write one ( Porting ) none yet Plain CMake no Plain CMake ( add_subdirectory() or find_package() , see Installation ) covers STM32, RP2040, nRF and host builds. docs.text: Porting to ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF ports in examples/esp32/main/esp32_se05x_port.hpp use the i2c_master driver for the bus, esp_timer for the clock and a GPIO for the reset port. This page says what each port must do for the SE05x and why. For another platform read Porting first. Datasheet sections this page relies on I2C target address 0x48: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, 4.1 I2C interfaces, Figure 3, p. 8 I2C clock and clock stretching per variant: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, 4.1.1 Supported I2C frequencies, p. 9 I2C.1 lock-up after a second command, I2C.2 no empty frame: NXP SE050_Erratasheet Rev. 1.0, 3.1, 3.2, p. 7 I2C.3 lines high around a soft reset, I2C.4 SCL before SDA: NXP SE050_Erratasheet Rev. 1.0, 3.3, 3.4, p. 8 One block per I2C write, no repeated start: NXP UM11225 Rev. 1.2, I2C framing, p. 13 Polling with one-byte reads after MPOT: NXP UM11225 Rev. 1.2, Polling, p. 14 Development kit jumpers: ENA, reset, pull-ups: NXP AN13539 Rev. 1.2, Table 9 and the jumper tables, p. 15 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Bus ¶ Setting Value Why Address 7-bit 0x48 SE050 section 4.1, p. 8 Clock 400 kHz Holds for every configuration. Above 600 kHz the A to D and F configurations stretch the clock (section 4.1.1, p. 9) Clock stretching allowed, with a timeout The chip may stretch; a stretch that never ends is errata I2C.1 and must come back as BusStuck , not hang Pull-ups external, on SDA and SCL Do not rely on the MCU's internal pull-ups; the vendor kit fits 3.3 kΩ (AN13539 p. 15) Rules the bus port keeps: One write per block. Write() is one i2c_master_transmit() : start, address, bytes, stop. No i2c_master_transmit_receive() : the T=1 link never uses a repeated start (UM11225 p. 13). Never empty. No zero-length write and no i2c_master_probe() on the chip's address: an address-only frame can hold the bus (errata I2C.2, p. 7). The driver's Write() never passes an empty span. Report a NAK as Nack . While the chip works it NAKs its address; the link polls after MPOT (UM11225 p. 14). Map ESP_ERR_TIMEOUT to Timeout and a stuck line to BusStuck , so the ladder can act. Keep the lines high. After a soft reset both lines must be high for at least 1 ms (errata I2C.3, p. 8). Do not drive SDA or SCL low from software, and keep the bus free of other devices that hold it. SCL before SDA. The SE050 needs SCL to change before SDA with a margin (errata I2C.4, p. 8). Check that your controller's data hold time gives that margin; a bit-banged port must add a delay. Clock ¶ NowUs() is esp_timer_get_time() , which is monotonic; DelayUs() may yield to other tasks. Waits are short (MPOT is 1 ms), so a task delay with a 1 ms tick is enough. Reset port ¶ Chip Pin SetEnable(false) PowerCycle() Reset() SE050, SE051 ENA, VOUT wired to VCC ( Esp32Se05xPins::enable , GPIO11 by default) ENA low: deep power-down ENA low 10 us (tENalt is 2 us typical, no minimum printed), then high, then the boot wait the ENA power cycle: RST_N has no effect with I2C alone SE052 RST_N ( Esp32Se05xPins::reset_n ; enable -1) not available (no ENA) supply switch, if the board has one (the example port returns false) RST_N low at least 40 us Sources: SE050 sections 4.2 and 5.2 and Table 14 (pp. 9, 10, 18); SE052 Table 2 and Table 14 (pp. 4, 20). A board without the reset port loses the power-cycle rung: a bus held by errata I2C.1 then stays held until the supply is switched. On the vendor development kit ENA and the reset line reach the Arduino header through jumpers (AN13539 p. 15). Crypto port ¶ Bind the crypto port to mbedTLS or PSA on the target, never to the driver's ReferenceCrypto in a product: the optional examples/psa/se05x_psa_crypto.hpp does it over PSA Crypto, which the ESP-IDF mbedtls component provides ( se05x_hrot_example uses it; add mbedtls to the component's REQUIRES ). Keep the platform SCP03 keys in NVS encryption or a key store and give the driver only KeyRef handles. Never compile keys into the image. Concurrency ¶ One command in flight: guard every call on one device with one mutex, or use it from one task. Two chips on two buses are independent. Bench status: not verified on hardware . The bench steps: an OM-SE050ARD on an ESP32 at 400 kHz, Open() , GetRandom() , a forced I2C.1 lock-up (two writes without a read) recovered by the ENA power cycle.

docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing small port classes. Datasheet sections this page relies on RST_N has no effect when only I2C is enabled: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, 4.2 ISO7816 and ISO14443 interface, p. 9 ENA low time and glitches: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, Table 14 AC characteristics, p. 18 SE052 RST_N reset pulse width: NXP SE052 Rev. 1.5, Table 14 AC characteristics, p. 20 I2C.1 lock-up after a second command, I2C.2 no empty frame: NXP SE050_Erratasheet Rev. 1.0, 3.1, 3.2, p. 7 I2C.3 lines high around a soft reset, I2C.4 SCL before SDA: NXP SE050_Erratasheet Rev. 1.0, 3.3, 3.4, p. 8 One block per I2C write, no repeated start: NXP UM11225 Rev. 1.2, I2C framing, p. 13 Polling with one-byte reads after MPOT: NXP UM11225 Rev. 1.2, Polling, p. 14 Timeouts and waiting time extensions: NXP AN13030 Rev. 2.7, 2.10, p. 9 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on classes you derive from the CRTP bases in inc/se05x_ports.hpp ; the Ports<...> bundle is constrained by concepts, so calls resolve at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error. What you implement ¶ Port Required Hooks BusInterface<D> yes bool EnsureInitialized() , BusStatus Write(addr7, ByteSpan) , BusRead Read(addr7, MutableByteSpan) ClockInterface<D> yes uint64_t NowUs() , void DelayUs(uint32_t) CryptoInterface<D> yes key handles, AES, CMAC, P-256, hash, random; ReferenceCrypto is for tests and bring-up only. Its only verifier is P-256 ( EcdsaP256Verify ), which is all the driver and the facade need; a P-384 certificate chain needs a verifier of yours ( PKI ) ResetInterface<D> no Reset() , PowerCycle() , SetEnable(bool) ; without it the power-cycle rung is gone. Reset() must really reset the chip: on the SE050 and SE051 the ENA power cycle (VOUT wired to VCC), because RST_N does nothing with I2C alone; on the SE052 RST_N, which has no ENA LogInterface<D> no Log(const LogRecord&) ; records never carry secrets The bus reads and writes are separate transactions ( kRepeatedStart is false), at up to kMaxClockHz . A Nack means the chip is not ready; the link polls. class MyBus : public se05x :: BusInterface < MyBus > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return true ; // set up the I2C controller here; return false when it cannot start } se05x :: BusStatus Write ( uint8_t addr7 , se05x :: ByteSpan data ) noexcept { static_cast < void > ( addr7 ); static_cast < void > ( data ); return se05x :: BusStatus :: Ok ; // one I2C write transaction; Nack when the chip does not answer } se05x :: BusRead Read ( uint8_t addr7 , se05x :: MutableByteSpan out ) noexcept { static_cast < void > ( addr7 ); static_cast < void > ( out ); return se05x :: BusRead { se05x :: BusStatus :: Nack , 0U }; // Nack while the chip is not ready } }; class MyClock : public se05x :: ClockInterface < MyClock > { public : uint64_t NowUs () noexcept { return 0U ; // a monotonic microsecond counter } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { static_cast < void > ( us ); // block for at least `us` microseconds } }; What the bus port must guarantee ¶ One block is one write: start, address, bytes, stop; never a repeated start (UM11225 p. 13). Never a zero-length write or an address-only probe on the chip's address (errata I2C.2, p. 7). A NAK of the address comes back as Nack (the chip is busy; the link polls after MPOT, UM11225 p. 14); a line held low comes back as BusStuck , a bounded wait as Timeout . Never block forever on clock stretching. SDA and SCL stay high while idle and around resets (errata I2C.3, p. 8); SCL changes before SDA with the data sheet margin (errata I2C.4, p. 8). One command in flight per device: the driver is not thread-safe (errata I2C.1). If your bus driver reports a NACK, a lost arbitration and a held line with one error code (ESP-IDF does), look at the lines after a failed transaction: SDA or SCL still low is BusStuck (the ESP-IDF example does this). What the clock port must guarantee ¶ NowUs() is monotonic and counts microseconds in 64 bits from boot, and never wraps in the life of the device. Every deadline in the link is an absolute 64-bit time compared with NowUs() ; a clock that wraps would end or stretch a wait at the wrap. A 32-bit microsecond counter wraps every 71.6 minutes: widen it in the port (count the wraps) rather than pass it through. DelayUs() waits at least the time asked; the driver bounds every wait, so a longer delay only slows it down. The reset port ¶ PowerCycle() is the last rung of the recovery ladder and the only cure for a bus held by errata I2C.1. On the SE050 and SE051 implement it with ENA: low for well above tENalt, which SE050 Table 14 (p. 18) gives as 2 us typical with no minimum (the ESP-IDF example holds 10 us), then high, with VOUT wired to VCC so the core really loses power. On the SE052 use a supply switch if the board has one, and Reset() with RST_N (at least 40 us low, SE052 Table 14, p. 20). A step-by-step ESP-IDF port: Porting to ESP-IDF . An ESP-IDF set of ports is in examples/esp32/main/esp32_se05x_port.hpp . Hardware crypto: implement CryptoInterface over your engine so keys never leave it.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ Run the driver on your PC first, with no hardware; then open the chip from your MCU: wire it, write two small ports, call Open() . Try it on your PC ¶ examples/host/ runs the facade jobs against the simulated chip of the tests, then shows what a bus with nothing on it gives. docs.text: Recurring defects ¶ The defects that reached an independent reviewer or the first CI run of more than one driver, one entry per class. Review skills cite these ids; the mechanization policy says where each class is caught and when it moves up a level. Append new findings to the entry they belong to, or add an entry (see the policy). Evidence names the driver, the review round ( reviews/<driver>-review<N>.md , finding id) or the CI run ( reports/<driver>-ci-*.txt ). Code examples are generic and minimal; none quotes a datasheet or a standard. Detection levels: lint (a script in the preflight or the gate, no judgement), test (a model knob, a mutation, a fuzz property or a compile-fail case that fails when the defect is present), review (a named reviewer asks one question). Status: enforced is in the template now; planned is the target, tracked in the policy's backlog, and until it lands the level below it (test, then review) is what protects the driver. data 3 review test RD-04 Invalid argument still sends something 2 test test RD-05 Stop, switch-off or release refused 4 review test RD-06 Transfer buffers on the stack 4 review test RD-07 Chip model shares the driver's misreading 2 review lint + review RD-08 False coverage matrix or fuzz claim 3 review lint RD-09 Docs promise behaviour the code lacks 6 review review (claims check) RD-10 Incomplete state-machine guard 5 review test RD-11 Header outside the library subset 2 lint lint RD-12 Rule 7.0.3 character arithmetic 3 CI lint RD-13 Rule 8.0.1 missing parentheses 2 CI lint RD-14 Rule 9.4.1 else-less chain 3 CI lint RD-15 Rule 0.1.2 unused return value 1 CI lint RD-16 Rule 13.3.3 parameter names differ 1 CI lint RD-17 Rule 7.0.6 literal argument type 4 review lint (partial) + review RD-18 Advisories 6.9.2, 15.1.4, 0.0.2 5 CI lint (known list) RD-19 Template drift 3 lint lint RD-20 ESP-IDF REQUIRES incomplete 1 CI lint RD-21 ESP32 example cannot start with its defaults 3 Guards no test kills (surviving mutants) 6 review test RD-26 Fuzz target does not check the safety rules 3 review test RD-27 Local tidy and format differ from CI 4 CI lint RD-28 Datasheet misread in a decode, clear or timing 6 review review RD-29 Hardware doc exceeds a datasheet limit 3 review review RD-30 Out-of-bounds or UB before a guard 3 test test RD-31 Clear-on-read flags lost by a diagnostic
