Wiring the SE052 Figure description and sources The SE052 on an MCU's I2C bus. SDA (pin 11) and SCL (pin 10) go to the MCU with pull-ups to the bus supply of 1.65 V to 3.6 V, which also feeds VIN (pin 12). VOUT (pin 15) goes to VDD (pin 18) on the board, as Table 2 asks; Figure 1 shows an optional 22 nF on VIN and an optional 22 nF (or nothing) on VOUT. RST_N (pin 14) goes to a GPIO the reset port drives low to reset the chip. There is no ENA pin: deep power-down is the S-block 0xDF, and the next I2C access wakes the chip. CLK (13) is left open or tied to ground, LA and LB are left open, IO1 and IO2 are the chip's own I2C controller and stay open when it is not used. The pull-up value is not in the data sheet. Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/se052-wiring.py . What differs by applet ¶ 3.x (SE050 A to D, F): attestation format 1 (nonce echo), ECDAA, no AES-GCM or CCM, 2-byte free-memory reply. The HRoT facade ( hrot::Device ) does not run here: every facade call returns Unsupported before anything is sent, after its argument checks (an invalid key, an off-curve point or an empty buffer is refused first with InvalidArgument ). Use se05x::Device directly on these chips. 6.x (SE051 A2 and C2 on early boards, OEF A565 and A564): no specification in hand; the policy builder uses the 3.x rule table. The HRoT facade does not run here either: every facade call returns Unsupported before anything is sent, after the same argument checks. Use se05x::Device , or update the applet to 7.x. 7.x (SE050E, SE051, SE052): the HRoT facade runs; attestation format 2 (the command is signed), AES-GCM, CCM and GMAC, Curve448 on SE050E and SE051, PAKE on parts with the feature bits, ReadState, TriggerSelfTest, DisableObjectCreation; the extended version carries 30 feature bytes (AN12543 Table 9). FIPS modes : the SE050F refuses RSA 1024, plain RSA, 2-key 3DES, SHA-1 signatures and curves under 224 bits; the SE052F has no EdDSA, Montgomery curves, DES, MIFARE DESFire or PAKE (AN12543 3.13.2 FIPS 140-3 mode, p. 45). The driver reads the chip, not the name ¶ Open() reads the applet version and AppletConfig, the extended feature bits on 7.x, the OEF id and the free-memory width, and fills Capabilities . Every command passes the capability gate before it is sent: a command the chip does not have is Unsupported and costs no round trip. The OEF ids per configuration are in AN12436 Table 2 (SE050) and AN12973 Table 4 (SE051); where two tables of one note disagree, the chip's own value wins. Not for this driver ¶ The SE051P runs a customer applet and has no IoT applet. The T4T applet of the SE051H and the SEMS Lite update agent are outside v1 ( Limitations ).

docs.text: The family has three chips, many configurations and two applet generations. This page helps you choose where each fits and which one to order; the per-chip guides ( SE050 , SE051 , SE052 ) cover wiring and what differs. Datasheet sections this page relies on I2C clock and clock stretching per variant: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, 4.1.1 Supported I2C frequencies, p. 9 SE050 ordering and variants: NXP SE050-DATASHEET Rev. 3.8, Table 3 Ordering information, p. 10 SE051 ordering and variants: NXP SE051 Rev. 2.0, Table 2 Ordering information, p. 11 Feature bits of the extended version: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Table 9, p. 26 Limits of FIPS 140-3 mode: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, 3.13.2 FIPS 140-3 mode, p. 45 GetVersion, GetTimestamp, GetFreeMemory, GetRandom: NXP AN12543 Rev. 4.5, Generic management commands, p. 151 SE050 variant identifiers: NXP AN12436 Rev. 2.4, Table 2 Variant identifiers, p. 8 SE051 OEF identifiers per variant: NXP AN12973 Rev. 2.0, Table 4, p. 4 SE052F configuration: applet 7.2.22, AppletConfig 0x26F2, OEF B501: NXP AN14277 Rev. 1.0, SE052F configuration, p. 2 GetFreeMemory reply width: NXP AN13030 Rev. 2.7, GetFreeMemory, p. 641 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Choosing a variant, an applet and an authentication Figure description and sources Read top to bottom; take the first question you answer yes. Certification needs come first: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 is the SE052F; FIPS 140-2 with SCP03 mandatory is the SE050F. Then interfaces: NFC commissioning and Matter (PAKE) is the SE051H, UWB the SE051W. Field update of the applet (SEMS Lite) is the SE051A or C. Otherwise the SE050 by algorithm set: E for AES-GCM and CCM and Curve448 (applet 7.x), C for ECC and RSA, A for ECC only, B for RSA only, D for ECC with MIFARE DESFire. The SE051P runs a customer applet and has no IoT applet, so this driver does not apply. The bottom row is the authentication choice: platform SCP03 whenever the bus can be probed, an ECKey session to bind a host, a UserID session only under a trusted host OS, since it has no secure messaging. The driver reads the real capabilities at Open() and never trusts the part name. Drawn from: inc/se05x_types.hpp ; inc/se05x_caps.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/variant-decision.py .

docs.text: Figures ¶ Every figure on this site is drawn by a Python module from facts extracted from the code, so it is rebuilt, not redrawn, when the code changes. CI runs kokeb-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. ECDH key agreement ¶ ECDH key agreement Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Peer, Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Provision (slot 1) (once) to hrot::Device. Peer sends peer public key to Firmware. Firmware sends Agree(key, peer, SecretBuffer) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDHGenerateSharedSecret (encrypted both ways) to SE05x. SE05x returns shared secret (R-ENC, R-MAC) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns SecretBuffer, wiped on failure and at scope end to Firmware. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device says: HKDF, then AES-GCM with the derived key. Drawn from: docs/model/agree-call.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/agree-call.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/agree-call.seq.yml An attested read ¶ An attested read Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Attest(trusted attestation key, slot 0) to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: fresh 16-byte nonce from the host crypto port. hrot::Device sends ReadObject with attestation (nonce) to SE05x. SE05x returns value, unique id, timestamp, attributes, signature to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: check the command hash and the signature over the TLVs as returned. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: check a later timestamp and the unique id against this open's read. hrot::Device returns Verified , or an error to Firmware. The steps run from top to bottom. Device firmware sends generate the device key (inside the chip) to SE05x. Device firmware sends sign the CSR body (ECDSASign) to SE05x. Device firmware sends CSR with the unique id as serialNumber to Factory station. Factory station sends CSR to Your CA. Your CA returns device certificate, CA certificate to Factory station. Factory station sends both certificates to Device firmware. Device firmware sends WriteBinary: certificate and trust anchor (nobody may write them) to SE05x. Hardware description: docs/model/csr-flow.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/csr-flow.seq.yml The layers ¶ The layers Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/se05x_device.hpp public calls ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py Drawn from: public calls in inc/se05x_device.hpp ECKey session: opening it ¶ ECKey session: opening it Figure description and sources The driver's eckey layer, the crypto port and the IoT applet. The driver first reads the chip's ECKA public key with an attested ReadObject and verifies the attestation. The crypto port makes a fresh ephemeral P-256 key pair for this session only and signs the request with the host's long-term key, whose public half is the ECKey authentication object on the chip. ECKeySessionInternalAuthenticate (84 88) carries the parameters (tag A6), the ephemeral public key (tag 7F49) and the signature (tag 5F37). The chip answers a 16-byte challenge and a 16-byte receipt. The host computes the shared secret, derives the master key (the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 over a counter, the secret, the chip's random and the parameters) and the session keys by CMAC, and checks the receipt in constant time before it trusts the session. The ephemeral private key and the master key are wiped. AN12543 pp. 22-23, 33-34, 72-73; no vector confirms the derivation yet, so it is built behind a flag. Drawn from: inc/se05x_eckey.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/eckey-session.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/eckey-session.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_eckey.hpp The first 15 minutes ¶ The first 15 minutes Figure description and sources Four steps in order, each with its minutes. Run the host example takes minutes 0 to 3. Read what it did takes minutes 3 to 6. Wire the chip takes minutes 6 to 11. Flash the ESP32 example takes minutes 11 to 15. The first two steps need no hardware. Drawn from: docs/model/first-15-minutes.graph.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/first-15-minutes.graph.yml Drawn from: docs/model/first-15-minutes.graph.yml Irreversible operations: plan, confirm, apply ¶ Irreversible operations: plan, confirm, apply Figure description and sources Left to right. The build must define SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE, or none of these calls exists. The caller asks irreversible::Operations for a Plan of one operation: the Plan sends nothing, checks the arguments, the capabilities and the role, and says what will change. The caller shows the Plan to a person and builds a Confirmation of the same operation from its phrase. Apply() takes both; a Plan of another operation, a phrase of another operation or a Plan that was not prepared is refused before any byte is sent (Error::IrreversibleNotConfirmed). The operation tags are read from inc/se05x_confirm.hpp; the two PERSO operations live on perso::Perso and follow the same flow. Drawn from: inc/se05x_confirm.hpp operation tags ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/irreversible-flow.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/irreversible-flow.py Drawn from: operation tags in inc/se05x_confirm.hpp What the chip does for your firmware ¶ What the chip does for your firmware Figure description and sources Your firmware connects to the SE05x over I2C, T=1, SCP03. From the SE05x nine jobs follow. Root of trust is a device identity key that never leaves the chip. Secret storage holds a Wi-Fi passphrase, tokens and configuration. Certificates and signing covers CSR, chain and ECDSA. TLS and mutual-auth gives client credentials. Key agreement is ECDH with a peer. Secure sessions make the bus encrypted and authenticated. Attestation is a signed answer, checked on the host. Monotonic counters hold anti-rollback floors. Secure provisioning and lifecycle locks set up and lock a device. Drawn from: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml Drawn from: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml Lifecycle settings and the roles that change them ¶ Lifecycle settings and the roles that change them Figure description and sources The device-wide settings of the IoT applet, each changed by one command that the chip accepts only in a session opened with one reserved authentication object (the AuthRole of inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp, checked by RequiredRole() before anything is sent). Transport lock: SetLockState from a Transport session; while locked the chip answers only GetVersion, ReadState, the read of the unique id, GetRandom and CreateSession (AN12543 Table 19); the persistent lock survives resets and is lifted only from a Transport session again. Platform SCP required: SetPlatformSCPRequest from a PlatformScp session; from then on every command needs full platform SCP03. Restricted object creation: DisableObjectCreation; the persistent form cannot be undone. Applet features: SetAppletFeatures from a Feature (ECKey) session. Factory reset: DeleteAll from a FactoryReset session removes every object except the provisioned ones; its reply is not wrapped and the session ends. ReadState reads the first three at any time. Red arrows are the operations the driver treats as irreversible: they exist only with SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE and need a Plan and a Confirmation. Drawn from: inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp AuthRole ; inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp RequiredRole ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/lifecycle.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/lifecycle.py Drawn from: AuthRole in inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp RequiredRole in inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp Objects, policies and sessions ¶ Objects, policies and sessions Figure description and sources Every key or data item on the chip is a secure object: a 4-byte identifier, a class (ObjectClass of inc/se05x_ids.hpp), a lifetime (persistent, or transient: the content is lost at reset or deselect) and an origin (generated inside, written from outside, or provisioned by the vendor; attestation reports it). At creation the object gets a policy set: each policy names one authentication object and the operations it may do (the Rule enumeration of inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp, 9 to 53 bytes per policy; AN12543 Table 63). An authentication object is itself a secure object (a UserID, an AES key or an EC key); a session opened with it (at most 2 at a time) is what a policy checks. The policy builder only builds rules valid for the class and generation, and the facade uses the strict profile only. Drawn from: inc/se05x_ids.hpp ObjectClass, Origin, Lifetime ; inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp Rule ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/object-policy.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/object-policy.py Drawn from: ObjectClass, Origin, Lifetime in inc/se05x_ids.hpp Rule in inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp Device certificates: provision once, verify at boot ¶ Device certificates: provision once, verify at boot Figure description and sources Left to right, top row once in the factory, bottom row at every boot. 1. The chip generates the key pair; only the public key comes out (ReadPublicKey). 2. BuildCsr writes the request and the chip signs its digest (DeviceSigner); VerifyCsr checks it against its own key. 3. The CA, outside the driver, issues the certificate. 4. StoreCertificate writes the certificate and the CA certificate (the trust anchor) into new binary objects with read-only policies, in one WriteBinary each, and reads them back. At boot: ReadCertificate and LoadTrustAnchor read them, VerifyChain checks signature, names, time, constraints and path length with the caller's clock, and the verified key is the chip's own. The CA, revocation and TLS are outside the driver. Drawn from: inc/se05x_pki_csr.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_device.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_verify.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/pki-provisioning.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/pki-provisioning.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_pki_csr.hpp inc/se05x_pki_device.hpp inc/se05x_pki_verify.hpp The factory provisioning flow ¶ The factory provisioning flow Figure description and sources Seven steps in order. Open with the product's platform keys, never the vendor defaults. CheckPlan, then Provision the sign, TLS and agree keys. FactoryRecord: Identify, public keys, attestation. CSR, certificates and trust anchor. CreateCounter makes the anti-rollback floors. Store the network credentials. Then the question Lock? has two answers. Plan, read and confirm leads to Irreversible: RequirePlatformScp, SetLockStatePersistent and DisableObjectCreation. Not yet leads to Ship unlocked, for development only. Drawn from: docs/model/provisioning-flow.graph.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/provisioning-flow.graph.yml Drawn from: docs/model/provisioning-flow.graph.yml The recovery ladder ¶ The recovery ladder Figure description and sources When an exchange fails the link climbs these rungs in order, read from the Rung enumeration in inc/se05x_t1.hpp, and stops at the first that works. Each rung is bounded and is never repeated without limit. Resending the last block keeps everything. A resync and an interface soft reset keep the chip's state but drop the exchange in progress. Selecting the applet again closes the applet sessions. The chip reset (the NXP-flavour S-block 0xC6, or the reset port in the GP flavour, where 0xC6 means RELEASE) also clears transient objects, and is the only answer to SW 0x66A6. The power cycle needs the reset port (ENA with VOUT wired to VCC on the SE050 and SE051) and is the only cure for errata I2C.1. After any rung past the resend, the driver forgets every session and the caller authenticates again (Error::Resynced). Drawn from: inc/se05x_t1.hpp Rung ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/recovery-ladder.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/recovery-ladder.py Drawn from: Rung in inc/se05x_t1.hpp The anti-rollback boot check ¶ The anti-rollback boot check Figure description and sources Boot image version v enters the check CheckFloor(floor, v). If v is below the floor the answer is PolicyDenied and the flow ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. If the answer is Ok the flow continues to Run the self test. When the test passed, RaiseCounterTo(floor, v) raises the floor in one command. When it failed, the flow also ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. Drawn from: docs/model/rollback-flow.graph.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/rollback-flow.graph.yml Drawn from: docs/model/rollback-flow.graph.yml Opening an SCP03 session ¶ Opening an SCP03 session Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Device::Open, Crypto port and SE05x card manager. The steps run from top to bottom. Device::Open sends host challenge (Random) to Crypto port. Device::Open sends INITIALIZE UPDATE (host challenge) to SE05x card manager. SE05x card manager returns card challenge, card cryptogram to Device::Open. Device::Open sends derive S-ENC, S-MAC, S-RMAC (CMAC KDF) to Crypto port. A note over Device::Open and SE05x card manager says: Device::Open: check the card cryptogram. Device::Open sends EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATE (host cryptogram, level) to SE05x card manager. A note over Device::Open and SE05x card manager says: from here every command: C-MAC (+ C-DEC); every answer: R-MAC (+ R-ENC). Drawn from: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml Platform SCP03: opening the channel ¶ Platform SCP03: opening the channel Figure description and sources Three parties, left to right: the driver's scp03 layer, the crypto port that holds the static platform keys as handles, and the chip's card manager. The driver sends INITIALIZE UPDATE with a host challenge; the chip answers with its challenge and card cryptogram. The crypto port derives the session keys from the static keys (the driver never sees them) and the driver checks the card cryptogram in constant time. EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATE carries the host cryptogram and the security level; when platform SCP is required the level must be full C-MAC, C-ENC, R-MAC and R-ENC (AN12543 SetPlatformSCPRequest, p. 75). Every later APDU is wrapped (C-MAC, C-ENC) and every reply checked (R-MAC, R-ENC); a failed check closes the channel and wipes the keys. The normative SCP03 text is the GlobalPlatform SCP03 amendment, which is not in this driver's source set: the byte detail follows AN12543 p. 72 and the middleware oracle. Drawn from: inc/se05x_scp03.hpp SecurityLevel ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/scp03-session.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/scp03-session.py Drawn from: SecurityLevel in inc/se05x_scp03.hpp SE052 package outline, HVQFN20 ¶ SE052 package outline, HVQFN20 Figure description and sources The SE052 body from above and from the side, to one scale: 4.0 x 4.0 mm, 0.85 mm high, 20 pins at a 0.5 mm pitch, five on each side, pin 1 at the top of the left side (SE052 data sheet section 6, p. 5, and the pin order of Table 2, p. 4). The terminal and exposed-pad dimensions are in the package drawing SOT917-7, not in the data sheet, so the pins are drawn as position marks only. The SE050 and SE051 come in the smaller HX2QFN20 (3.0 x 3.0 x 0.32 mm, 0.4 mm pitch). Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/se052-outline.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/se052-outline.py Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py SE052 pinout, HVQFN20 ¶ SE052 pinout, HVQFN20 Figure description and sources The SE052 seen from the top in its HVQFN20 package (4 x 4 x 0.85 mm, 0.5 mm pitch, SOT917-7 in the data sheet). Pin 1 is at the top of the left side and the numbers run counter-clockwise: 1 to 5 down the left side, 6 to 10 along the bottom, 11 to 15 up the right side and 16 to 20 along the top. Each pin card is coloured by the pin's type as in the HX2QFN20 pinout. The driver uses SDA (11) and SCL (10) for the bus and RST_N (14) through the reset port; the SE052 has no ENA pin, so deep power-down is a T=1 S-block (0xDF) and the next I2C access wakes it. The table is SE052 Table 2 (p. 4). Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/se052-pinout.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/se052-pinout.py Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py Wiring the SE052 ¶ Wiring the SE052 Figure description and sources The SE052 on an MCU's I2C bus. SDA (pin 11) and SCL (pin 10) go to the MCU with pull-ups to the bus supply of 1.65 V to 3.6 V, which also feeds VIN (pin 12). VOUT (pin 15) goes to VDD (pin 18) on the board, as Table 2 asks; Figure 1 shows an optional 22 nF on VIN and an optional 22 nF (or nothing) on VOUT. RST_N (pin 14) goes to a GPIO the reset port drives low to reset the chip. There is no ENA pin: deep power-down is the S-block 0xDF, and the next I2C access wakes the chip. CLK (13) is left open or tied to ground, LA and LB are left open, IO1 and IO2 are the chip's own I2C controller and stay open when it is not used. The pull-up value is not in the data sheet. Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/se052-wiring.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/se052-wiring.py Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py Provision a signing key, then sign ¶ Provision a signing key, then sign Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Provision (slot 0) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends CheckObjectExists, WriteECKey (no key bytes, strict policy) to SE05x. A note over SE05x and hrot::Device says: the key pair is generated inside the chip. Firmware sends Sign(key, SHA-256 digest) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDSASign to SE05x. SE05x returns DER signature (R-MAC checked) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns Signature to Firmware. Drawn from: docs/model/sign-call.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/sign-call.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/sign-call.seq.yml Store a secret, load it at every boot ¶ Store a secret, load it at every boot Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. A note over Firmware and SE05x says: provisioning, once. Firmware sends Store(slot 1, passphrase, Secret) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends CheckObjectExists, WriteBinary (encrypted, MACed) to SE05x. SE05x returns 9000 (R-MAC checked) to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and SE05x says: every boot. Firmware sends Load(slot 1, buffer, Secret) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ReadSize, ReadObject (encrypted) to SE05x. SE05x returns the bytes (R-ENC, R-MAC) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns SecretBuffer, wiped when it goes out of scope to Firmware. Drawn from: docs/model/store-load-call.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/store-load-call.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/store-load-call.seq.yml One T=1 block on the bus ¶ One T=1 block on the bus Figure description and sources One block on the I2C bus, in the order its bytes are sent, for each flavour the driver speaks. The NXP flavour (UM11225) has NAD 0x5A from the host and 0xA5 from the chip, a one-byte LEN and at most 254 bytes of INF. The GlobalPlatform flavour (GPC_SPE_172) has NAD 0x21 and 0x12, a two-byte big-endian LEN and up to 4089 bytes of INF. Both end with a CRC-16 over NAD to INF; in the GP flavour it is CRC-16/X-25 sent most significant byte first (the document's example block ends in BDA4); UM11225 gives neither the polynomial's byte order nor an example, so the link tries both orders and keeps the first that checks. The PCB byte tells the three kinds of block apart. Every number is read from inc/se05x_wire.hpp. Drawn from: inc/se05x_wire.hpp kUm11225Frame, kGpFrame, kGpExampleCrc ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/t1-frame.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/t1-frame.py Drawn from: kUm11225Frame, kGpFrame, kGpExampleCrc in inc/se05x_wire.hpp The T=1 link: states and S-blocks ¶ The T=1 link: states and S-blocks Figure description and sources Each box is a LinkState of t1::Link, read from inc/se05x_t1.hpp. Open() reads the ATR or CIP and selects the applet, leaving the link Idle. A command makes it InFlight: one I-block per I2C write (chained when the APDU is longer than IFSC, each part acknowledged by an R-block), then the reply is polled. While in flight the chip may ask for more time with S(WTX request), which the link answers with S(WTX response), counted against Config::wtx_limit; a bad block gets an R-block and is resent at most Config::frame_retries times. A reply returns the link to Idle. A rung of the recovery ladder that resets the chip's context leaves NeedsReselect, which selecting the applet again ends; when the ladder is spent the link is Dead and only Close() and Open() start it again. The S-block codes are the ones of inc/se05x_wire.hpp; 0xC6 is a chip reset in the NXP flavour and RELEASE in the GP one. Drawn from: inc/se05x_t1.hpp LinkState ; inc/se05x_wire.hpp S-block codes ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/t1-states.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/t1-states.py Drawn from: LinkState in inc/se05x_t1.hpp S-block codes in inc/se05x_wire.hpp A TLS client signature ¶ A TLS client signature Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Server, TLS stack, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Server sends CertificateRequest to TLS stack. TLS stack sends client certificate (read from the chip's binary object) to Server. TLS stack sends TlsSign(key, handshake digest) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDSASign (secure messaging) to SE05x. SE05x returns signature to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns DER signature to TLS stack. TLS stack sends CertificateVerify to Server. Drawn from: docs/model/tls-sign-call.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/tls-sign-call.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/tls-sign-call.seq.yml Trust boundaries ¶ Trust boundaries Figure description and sources Three zones from right to left. Inside the chip: the private keys, the policies, the counters, the RNG and the attestation key; the chip enforces every access rule. The bus between host and chip carries APDUs in clear unless a secure channel (platform SCP03, an AESKey or an ECKey session) wraps them; anyone with a probe on SDA and SCL sees and can inject plain traffic. The host MCU runs this driver, which is a courier: it holds no long-term secret except the platform SCP03 keys, and those only as handles in the crypto port. The verifier, far left, checks attestations and signatures with public keys only. Each arrow says what crosses the boundary. Drawn from: inc/se05x_ports.hpp ; inc/se05x_secret.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/trust-boundaries.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/trust-boundaries.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_ports.hpp inc/se05x_secret.hpp Choosing a variant, an applet and an authentication ¶ Choosing a variant, an applet and an authentication Figure description and sources Read top to bottom; take the first question you answer yes. Certification needs come first: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 is the SE052F; FIPS 140-2 with SCP03 mandatory is the SE050F. Then interfaces: NFC commissioning and Matter (PAKE) is the SE051H, UWB the SE051W. Field update of the applet (SEMS Lite) is the SE051A or C. Otherwise the SE050 by algorithm set: E for AES-GCM and CCM and Curve448 (applet 7.x), C for ECC and RSA, A for ECC only, B for RSA only, D for ECC with MIFARE DESFire. The SE051P runs a customer applet and has no IoT applet, so this driver does not apply. The bottom row is the authentication choice: platform SCP03 whenever the bus can be probed, an ECKey session to bind a host, a UserID session only under a trusted host OS, since it has no secure messaging. The driver reads the real capabilities at Open() and never trusts the part name. Drawn from: inc/se05x_types.hpp ; inc/se05x_caps.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/variant-decision.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/variant-decision.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_types.hpp inc/se05x_caps.hpp

docs.text: ECDH key agreement Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Peer, Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Device firmware sends generate the device key (inside the chip) to SE05x. Device firmware sends sign the CSR body (ECDSASign) to SE05x. docs.text: The layers Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Drawn from: inc/se05x_device.hpp public calls ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . docs.text: ECKey session: opening it Figure description and sources The driver's eckey layer, the crypto port and the IoT applet. The driver first reads the chip's ECKA public key with an attested ReadObject and verifies the attestation. The crypto port makes a fresh ephemeral P-256 key pair for this session only and signs the request with the host's long-term key, whose public half is the ECKey authentication object on the chip. ECKeySessionInternalAuthenticate (84 88) carries the parameters (tag A6), the ephemeral public key (tag 7F49) and the signature (tag 5F37). The chip answers a 16-byte challenge and a 16-byte receipt. The host computes the shared secret, derives the master key (the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 over a counter, the secret, the chip's random and the parameters) and the session keys by CMAC, and checks the receipt in constant time before it trusts the session. The ephemeral private key and the master key are wiped. AN12543 pp. 22-23, 33-34, 72-73; no vector confirms the derivation yet, so it is built behind a flag. Drawn from: inc/se05x_eckey.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/eckey-session.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/eckey-session.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_eckey.hpp

docs.text: Irreversible operations: plan, confirm, apply Figure description and sources Left to right. The build must define SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE, or none of these calls exists. The caller asks irreversible::Operations for a Plan of one operation: the Plan sends nothing, checks the arguments, the capabilities and the role, and says what will change. The caller shows the Plan to a person and builds a Confirmation of the same operation from its phrase. Apply() takes both; a Plan of another operation, a phrase of another operation or a Plan that was not prepared is refused before any byte is sent (Error::IrreversibleNotConfirmed). The operation tags are read from inc/se05x_confirm.hpp; the two PERSO operations live on perso::Perso and follow the same flow. docs.text: What the chip does for your firmware Figure description and sources Your firmware connects to the SE05x over I2C, T=1, SCP03. From the SE05x nine jobs follow. Root of trust is a device identity key that never leaves the chip. Secret storage holds a Wi-Fi passphrase, tokens and configuration. Certificates and signing covers CSR, chain and ECDSA. TLS and mutual-auth gives client credentials. Key agreement is ECDH with a peer. Secure sessions make the bus encrypted and authenticated. Attestation is a signed answer, checked on the host. Monotonic counters hold anti-rollback floors. Secure provisioning and lifecycle locks set up and lock a device. Drawn from: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml Drawn from: docs/model/jobs-map.graph.yml

docs.text: Lifecycle settings and the roles that change them Figure description and sources The device-wide settings of the IoT applet, each changed by one command that the chip accepts only in a session opened with one reserved authentication object (the AuthRole of inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp, checked by RequiredRole() before anything is sent). Transport lock: SetLockState from a Transport session; while locked the chip answers only GetVersion, ReadState, the read of the unique id, GetRandom and CreateSession (AN12543 Table 19); the persistent lock survives resets and is lifted only from a Transport session again. Platform SCP required: SetPlatformSCPRequest from a PlatformScp session; from then on every command needs full platform SCP03. Restricted object creation: DisableObjectCreation; the persistent form cannot be undone. Applet features: SetAppletFeatures from a Feature (ECKey) session. Factory reset: DeleteAll from a FactoryReset session removes every object except the provisioned ones; its reply is not wrapped and the session ends. ReadState reads the first three at any time. Red arrows are the operations the driver treats as irreversible: they exist only with SE05X_ENABLE_IRREVERSIBLE and need a Plan and a Confirmation. Drawn from: inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp AuthRole ; inc/se05x_lifecycle.hpp RequiredRole ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/lifecycle.py . docs.text: Objects, policies and sessions Figure description and sources Every key or data item on the chip is a secure object: a 4-byte identifier, a class (ObjectClass of inc/se05x_ids.hpp), a lifetime (persistent, or transient: the content is lost at reset or deselect) and an origin (generated inside, written from outside, or provisioned by the vendor; attestation reports it). At creation the object gets a policy set: each policy names one authentication object and the operations it may do (the Rule enumeration of inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp, 9 to 53 bytes per policy; AN12543 Table 63). An authentication object is itself a secure object (a UserID, an AES key or an EC key); a session opened with it (at most 2 at a time) is what a policy checks. The policy builder only builds rules valid for the class and generation, and the facade uses the strict profile only. Drawn from: inc/se05x_ids.hpp ObjectClass, Origin, Lifetime ; inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp Rule ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/object-policy.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/object-policy.py Drawn from: ObjectClass, Origin, Lifetime in inc/se05x_ids.hpp Rule in inc/se05x_policy_types.hpp

docs.text: Device certificates: provision once, verify at boot Figure description and sources Left to right, top row once in the factory, bottom row at every boot. 1. The chip generates the key pair; only the public key comes out (ReadPublicKey). 2. BuildCsr writes the request and the chip signs its digest (DeviceSigner); VerifyCsr checks it against its own key. 3. The CA, outside the driver, issues the certificate. 4. StoreCertificate writes the certificate and the CA certificate (the trust anchor) into new binary objects with read-only policies, in one WriteBinary each, and reads them back. At boot: ReadCertificate and LoadTrustAnchor read them, VerifyChain checks signature, names, time, constraints and path length with the caller's clock, and the verified key is the chip's own. The CA, revocation and TLS are outside the driver. Drawn from: inc/se05x_pki_csr.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_device.hpp ; inc/se05x_pki_verify.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/pki-provisioning.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/pki-provisioning.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_pki_csr.hpp inc/se05x_pki_device.hpp inc/se05x_pki_verify.hpp

docs.text: The factory provisioning flow Figure description and sources Seven steps in order. Open with the product's platform keys, never the vendor defaults. CheckPlan, then Provision the sign, TLS and agree keys. FactoryRecord: Identify, public keys, attestation. CSR, certificates and trust anchor. CreateCounter makes the anti-rollback floors. Store the network credentials. Then the question Lock? has two answers. Plan, read and confirm leads to Irreversible: RequirePlatformScp, SetLockStatePersistent and DisableObjectCreation. Not yet leads to Ship unlocked, for development only. Drawn from: docs/model/provisioning-flow.graph.yml . docs.text: The recovery ladder Figure description and sources When an exchange fails the link climbs these rungs in order, read from the Rung enumeration in inc/se05x_t1.hpp, and stops at the first that works. Each rung is bounded and is never repeated without limit. Resending the last block keeps everything. A resync and an interface soft reset keep the chip's state but drop the exchange in progress. Selecting the applet again closes the applet sessions. The chip reset (the NXP-flavour S-block 0xC6, or the reset port in the GP flavour, where 0xC6 means RELEASE) also clears transient objects, and is the only answer to SW 0x66A6. The power cycle needs the reset port (ENA with VOUT wired to VCC on the SE050 and SE051) and is the only cure for errata I2C.1. After any rung past the resend, the driver forgets every session and the caller authenticates again (Error::Resynced). Drawn from: inc/se05x_t1.hpp Rung ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/recovery-ladder.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/recovery-ladder.py Drawn from: Rung in inc/se05x_t1.hpp
docs.title: The recovery ladder

docs.text: The anti-rollback boot check Figure description and sources Boot image version v enters the check CheckFloor(floor, v). If v is below the floor the answer is PolicyDenied and the flow ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. If the answer is Ok the flow continues to Run the self test. When the test passed, RaiseCounterTo(floor, v) raises the floor in one command. When it failed, the flow also ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. docs.text: Opening an SCP03 session Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Device::Open, Crypto port and SE05x card manager. The steps run from top to bottom. Device::Open sends host challenge (Random) to Crypto port. Device::Open sends INITIALIZE UPDATE (host challenge) to SE05x card manager. SE05x card manager returns card challenge, card cryptogram to Device::Open. Device::Open sends derive S-ENC, S-MAC, S-RMAC (CMAC KDF) to Crypto port. A note over Device::Open and SE05x card manager says: Device::Open: check the card cryptogram. Device::Open sends EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATE (host cryptogram, level) to SE05x card manager. A note over Device::Open and SE05x card manager says: from here every command: C-MAC (+ C-DEC); every answer: R-MAC (+ R-ENC). Drawn from: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml . Hardware description: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml Drawn from: docs/model/scp03-open.seq.yml
docs.title: Opening an SCP03 session

docs.text: Platform SCP03: opening the channel Figure description and sources Three parties, left to right: the driver's scp03 layer, the crypto port that holds the static platform keys as handles, and the chip's card manager. The driver sends INITIALIZE UPDATE with a host challenge; the chip answers with its challenge and card cryptogram. The crypto port derives the session keys from the static keys (the driver never sees them) and the driver checks the card cryptogram in constant time. EXTERNAL AUTHENTICATE carries the host cryptogram and the security level; when platform SCP is required the level must be full C-MAC, C-ENC, R-MAC and R-ENC (AN12543 SetPlatformSCPRequest, p. 75). Every later APDU is wrapped (C-MAC, C-ENC) and every reply checked (R-MAC, R-ENC); a failed check closes the channel and wipes the keys. The normative SCP03 text is the GlobalPlatform SCP03 amendment, which is not in this driver's source set: the byte detail follows AN12543 p. 72 and the middleware oracle. Drawn from: inc/se05x_scp03.hpp SecurityLevel ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/scp03-session.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/scp03-session.py Drawn from: SecurityLevel in inc/se05x_scp03.hpp

docs.text: SE052 pinout, HVQFN20 Figure description and sources The SE052 seen from the top in its HVQFN20 package (4 x 4 x 0.85 mm, 0.5 mm pitch, SOT917-7 in the data sheet). Pin 1 is at the top of the left side and the numbers run counter-clockwise: 1 to 5 down the left side, 6 to 10 along the bottom, 11 to 15 up the right side and 16 to 20 along the top. Each pin card is coloured by the pin's type as in the HX2QFN20 pinout. The driver uses SDA (11) and SCL (10) for the bus and RST_N (14) through the reset port; the SE052 has no ENA pin, so deep power-down is a T=1 S-block (0xDF) and the next I2C access wakes it. docs.text: Wiring the SE052 Figure description and sources The SE052 on an MCU's I2C bus. SDA (pin 11) and SCL (pin 10) go to the MCU with pull-ups to the bus supply of 1.65 V to 3.6 V, which also feeds VIN (pin 12). VOUT (pin 15) goes to VDD (pin 18) on the board, as Table 2 asks; Figure 1 shows an optional 22 nF on VIN and an optional 22 nF (or nothing) on VOUT. RST_N (pin 14) goes to a GPIO the reset port drives low to reset the chip. There is no ENA pin: deep power-down is the S-block 0xDF, and the next I2C access wakes the chip. CLK (13) is left open or tied to ground, LA and LB are left open, IO1 and IO2 are the chip's own I2C controller and stay open when it is not used. The pull-up value is not in the data sheet. Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/se052-wiring.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/se052-wiring.py Drawn from: docs/diagrams/figures/_se052.py

docs.text: Store a secret, load it at every boot Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. A note over Firmware and SE05x says: provisioning, once. Firmware sends Store(slot 1, passphrase, Secret) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends CheckObjectExists, WriteBinary (encrypted, MACed) to SE05x. SE05x returns 9000 (R-MAC checked) to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and SE05x says: every boot. Firmware sends Load(slot 1, buffer, Secret) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ReadSize, ReadObject (encrypted) to SE05x. docs.text: One T=1 block on the bus Figure description and sources One block on the I2C bus, in the order its bytes are sent, for each flavour the driver speaks. The NXP flavour (UM11225) has NAD 0x5A from the host and 0xA5 from the chip, a one-byte LEN and at most 254 bytes of INF. The GlobalPlatform flavour (GPC_SPE_172) has NAD 0x21 and 0x12, a two-byte big-endian LEN and up to 4089 bytes of INF. Both end with a CRC-16 over NAD to INF; in the GP flavour it is CRC-16/X-25 sent most significant byte first (the document's example block ends in BDA4); UM11225 gives neither the polynomial's byte order nor an example, so the link tries both orders and keeps the first that checks. The PCB byte tells the three kinds of block apart. Every number is read from inc/se05x_wire.hpp. Drawn from: inc/se05x_wire.hpp kUm11225Frame, kGpFrame, kGpExampleCrc ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/t1-frame.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/t1-frame.py Drawn from: kUm11225Frame, kGpFrame, kGpExampleCrc in inc/se05x_wire.hpp
docs.title: One T=1 block on the bus

docs.text: The T=1 link: states and S-blocks Figure description and sources Each box is a LinkState of t1::Link, read from inc/se05x_t1.hpp. Open() reads the ATR or CIP and selects the applet, leaving the link Idle. A command makes it InFlight: one I-block per I2C write (chained when the APDU is longer than IFSC, each part acknowledged by an R-block), then the reply is polled. While in flight the chip may ask for more time with S(WTX request), which the link answers with S(WTX response), counted against Config::wtx_limit; a bad block gets an R-block and is resent at most Config::frame_retries times. A reply returns the link to Idle. A rung of the recovery ladder that resets the chip's context leaves NeedsReselect, which selecting the applet again ends; when the ladder is spent the link is Dead and only Close() and Open() start it again. The S-block codes are the ones of inc/se05x_wire.hpp; 0xC6 is a chip reset in the NXP flavour and RELEASE in the GP one. Drawn from: inc/se05x_t1.hpp LinkState ; inc/se05x_wire.hpp S-block codes ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/t1-states.py . docs.text: Trust boundaries Figure description and sources Three zones from right to left. Inside the chip: the private keys, the policies, the counters, the RNG and the attestation key; the chip enforces every access rule. The bus between host and chip carries APDUs in clear unless a secure channel (platform SCP03, an AESKey or an ECKey session) wraps them; anyone with a probe on SDA and SCL sees and can inject plain traffic. The host MCU runs this driver, which is a courier: it holds no long-term secret except the platform SCP03 keys, and those only as handles in the crypto port. The verifier, far left, checks attestations and signatures with public keys only. Each arrow says what crosses the boundary. Drawn from: inc/se05x_ports.hpp ; inc/se05x_secret.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/trust-boundaries.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/trust-boundaries.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_ports.hpp inc/se05x_secret.hpp
docs.title: Trust boundaries

docs.text: Choosing a variant, an applet and an authentication Figure description and sources Read top to bottom; take the first question you answer yes. Certification needs come first: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 is the SE052F; FIPS 140-2 with SCP03 mandatory is the SE050F. Then interfaces: NFC commissioning and Matter (PAKE) is the SE051H, UWB the SE051W. Field update of the applet (SEMS Lite) is the SE051A or C. Otherwise the SE050 by algorithm set: E for AES-GCM and CCM and Curve448 (applet 7.x), C for ECC and RSA, A for ECC only, B for RSA only, D for ECC with MIFARE DESFire. The SE051P runs a customer applet and has no IoT applet, so this driver does not apply. The bottom row is the authentication choice: platform SCP03 whenever the bus can be probed, an ECKey session to bind a host, a UserID session only under a trusted host OS, since it has no secure messaging. The driver reads the real capabilities at Open() and never trusts the part name. Drawn from: inc/se05x_types.hpp ; inc/se05x_caps.hpp ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/variant-decision.py . Figure module: docs/diagrams/figures/variant-decision.py Drawn from: inc/se05x_types.hpp inc/se05x_caps.hpp
docs.title: Choosing a variant, an applet and an authentication

docs.text: Monotonic counters for anti-rollback ¶ A counter in the chip only counts up (WriteCounter, AN12543 p. 84). Use it as a floor: at boot refuse an image older than the floor, and after a new image has booted and passed its self test, raise the floor to its version. An attacker with full control of the host can neither count down nor delete the floor. The anti-rollback boot check Figure description and sources Boot image version v enters the check CheckFloor(floor, v). If v is below the floor the answer is PolicyDenied and the flow ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. If the answer is Ok the flow continues to Run the self test. When the test passed, RaiseCounterTo(floor, v) raises the floor in one command. When it failed, the flow also ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. Drawn from: docs/model/rollback-flow.graph.yml . /// The anti-rollback check at boot: refuse an image older than one that ran before. template < PortSet P > Error BootCheck ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , uint32_t image_version ) noexcept { constexpr hrot :: CounterSlot kFloor = hrot :: CounterSlot :: At < 0 > (); return hrot . CheckFloor ( kFloor , image_version ). error ; // Ok only when not below the floor } /// After the new image booted and passed its self test: raise the floor in one command. template < PortSet P > Error CommitImage ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , uint32_t image_version ) noexcept { return hrot . RaiseCounterTo ( hrot :: CounterSlot :: At < 0 > (), image_version ). error ; } The facade needs applet 7.x (SE050E, SE051, SE052): on applet 3.x (SE050 A to D and F) and 6.x (SE051 on early boards), CreateCounter , CheckFloor and RaiseCounterTo return Unsupported and send nothing, so a boot pattern written on them refuses every image. Use se05x::Device counters there. CreateCounter(slot, initial) makes the floor in one command with its start value, so a lost power cannot leave a floor of 0. Its policy grants delete to nobody: only a factory reset removes it. What it protects against ¶ Threat Answer Installing an old image with a known bug CheckFloor refuses a version below the floor ( PolicyDenied ) Lowering the floor The chip never lowers a counter Deleting the floor and creating it again lower The counter's policy grants delete to nobody Forging "Ok" on the bus Counter calls need authenticated answers (R-MAC) Raising the floor too far Not prevented. The counter's policy grants write, under secure messaging, to the default session and to the applet session the facade opened, because RaiseCounterTo and CounterIncrement need it. A host holding those keys can raise the floor to 0xFFFFFFFF; every later image is then refused and only a factory reset recovers the chip. This is a denial of service, not a rollback: keep the platform SCP03 keys out of reach of code that should not move the floor When it fails ¶ Error Meaning What to do PolicyDenied (layer Hrot , step 3) The version is below the floor Refuse the image PolicyDenied (layer Hrot , step 1) The answers are not authenticated Open platform SCP03 ObjectExists from CreateCounter The floor exists; it is now at least the value asked Nothing: keep booting FrameError The slot does not hold a 4-byte counter Treat as a rollback: refuse Bench step (not verified on hardware): create the floor at 3 on a dev kit, check version 4 passes and 2 is refused, raise to 4, power-cycle, and check 3 is refused.
docs.title: Anti-rollback

The anti-rollback boot check Figure description and sources Boot image version v enters the check CheckFloor(floor, v). If v is below the floor the answer is PolicyDenied and the flow ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. If the answer is Ok the flow continues to Run the self test. When the test passed, RaiseCounterTo(floor, v) raises the floor in one command. When it failed, the flow also ends at Refuse the image, boot the fallback. Drawn from: docs/model/rollback-flow.graph.yml . /// The anti-rollback check at boot: refuse an image older than one that ran before. template < PortSet P > Error BootCheck ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , uint32_t image_version ) noexcept { constexpr hrot :: CounterSlot kFloor = hrot :: CounterSlot :: At < 0 > (); return hrot . CheckFloor ( kFloor , image_version ). error ; // Ok only when not below the floor } /// After the new image booted and passed its self test: raise the floor in one command. template < PortSet P > Error CommitImage ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , uint32_t image_version ) noexcept { return hrot . RaiseCounterTo ( hrot :: CounterSlot :: At < 0 > (), image_version ). error ; } The facade needs applet 7.x (SE050E, SE051, SE052): on applet 3.x (SE050 A to D and F) and 6.x (SE051 on early boards), CreateCounter , CheckFloor and RaiseCounterTo return Unsupported and send nothing, so a boot pattern written on them refuses every image. Use se05x::Device counters there. CreateCounter(slot, initial) makes the floor in one command with its start value, so a lost power cannot leave a floor of 0. Its policy grants delete to nobody: only a factory reset removes it.
docs.title: Monotonic counters for anti-rollback

docs.text: Threat Answer Installing an old image with a known bug CheckFloor refuses a version below the floor ( PolicyDenied ) Lowering the floor The chip never lowers a counter Deleting the floor and creating it again lower The counter's policy grants delete to nobody Forging "Ok" on the bus Counter calls need authenticated answers (R-MAC) Raising the floor too far Not prevented. The counter's policy grants write, under secure messaging, to the default session and to the applet session the facade opened, because RaiseCounterTo and CounterIncrement need it. A host holding those keys can raise the floor to 0xFFFFFFFF; every later image is then refused and only a factory reset recovers the chip. This is a denial of service, not a rollback: keep the platform SCP03 keys out of reach of code that should not move the floor

docs.text: Error Meaning What to do PolicyDenied (layer Hrot , step 3) The version is below the floor Refuse the image PolicyDenied (layer Hrot , step 1) The answers are not authenticated Open platform SCP03 ObjectExists from CreateCounter The floor exists; it is now at least the value asked Nothing: keep booting FrameError The slot does not hold a 4-byte counter Treat as a rollback: refuse Bench step (not verified on hardware): create the floor at 3 on a dev kit, check version 4 passes and 2 is refused, raise to 4, power-cycle, and check 3 is refused.

docs.text: Attested reads: check a key on the host ¶ An attested read returns an object (here a public key) together with the chip's unique id, a timestamp and a signature by an attestation key; a format 2 signature covers the hash of the command the chip received and the returned TLVs (AN12543 3.2.7.2, p. 19). hrot::Device::Attest checks that answer on the host : your firmware learns that the value came, unchanged and fresh, from a chip that holds the attestation key you trust. An attested read Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Attest(trusted attestation key, slot 0) to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: fresh 16-byte nonce from the host crypto port. hrot::Device sends ReadObject with attestation (nonce) to SE05x. SE05x returns value, unique id, timestamp, attributes, signature to hrot::Device. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: check the command hash and the signature over the TLVs as returned. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device and SE05x says: hrot::Device: check a later timestamp and the unique id against this open's read. hrot::Device returns Verified , or an error to Firmware. Drawn from: docs/model/attest-call.seq.yml . /// Prove that the key in slot 0 lives in this chip. `vendor_public` must come from a verified /// certificate (the se05x::pki layer) or your factory record, never from the same chip. template < PortSet P > Error AttestDeviceKey ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , const hrot :: EcPublicKey & vendor_public , hrot :: EcPublicKey & attested_key ) noexcept { const auto trusted = hrot :: TrustAttestationKey ( FromReserved ( ReservedId :: RootOfTrustKey ), vendor_public ); if ( ! trusted . ok ()) { return trusted . error ; } const auto value = hrot . Attest ( trusted . value , hrot :: Slot :: At < 0 > ()); if ( ! value . ok ()) { return value . error ; // AttestationInvalid, Counterfeit: do not trust this chip } const hrot :: AttestedValue & checked = value . value . Get (); // a Verified<T> exists only if checked if ( checked . data . length != attested_key . point . size ()) { return Error :: FrameError ; // not an uncompressed P-256 point } for ( std :: size_t i = 0U ; i < attested_key . point . size (); ++ i ) { attested_key . point [ i ] = checked . data . bytes [ i ]; } return Error :: Ok ; } What the facade checks, and what it does not ¶ Checked by Attest Not checked by Attest The signature, with the attestation key you pass, over the hash of the command and the TLVs exactly as returned Whether the attestation key itself is genuine: that is the key you pass, so take it from the vendor certificate after its chain was verified ( CSR and certificates ), never from the same chip The command hash: the answer is for this request The object's class, origin or policy in the signed attributes: check them yourself when they matter ( Device::ReadAttested returns the attributes) A nonce from the host's crypto port for every request, and a timestamp later than the last one accepted, across reopens (AN12543 3.9, p. 42) Anything on a remote server: see below The unique id in the signed answer equals the one read from this chip in this open That the chip is genuine: a counterfeit chip with its own attestation key passes this check; only a trusted, vendor-chained attestation key defeats it Verified<AttestedValue> is a local result: it holds the value, the timestamp, the unique id and the object size, and no signature . For a data or certificate slot the value and object_size are without the completion marker of Store . The object is read whole in one attested read of at most kMaxAttestedBytes (256) bytes, marker included, so a stored value longer than 255 bytes cannot be attested ( BufferTooSmall ). The result cannot be sent to a server as proof, and a server cannot verify it. Proving the key to a server ¶ A server learns that a key lives in a genuine chip only by verifying the chip's signed answer itself, against the vendor's attestation certificate chain. The facade does not provide that. To build it, an integrator needs, beyond this driver: a request whose nonce the server chooses (the driver draws the nonce from the host's crypto port, so the server must trust the host, or the integration must pass the server's nonce through a crypto port that returns it); the signed answer as the chip returned it: Device::ReadAttested gives the value, the unique id, the timestamp, the signed attributes, the echoed command and the signature, but not the raw TLV bytes the format 2 signature covers; a server-side verifier of AN12543 3.2.7.2 with the vendor certificate chain (AN12436 Tables 8 and 9, p. 10). Until that exists, use attestation to check the chip on the host, and send the server a certificate for the key ( CSR and certificates ) issued at provisioning time, when the factory checked the attestation. When it fails ¶ Error Meaning What to do AttestationInvalid The signature, the command hash or the timestamp is wrong Do not trust the value Counterfeit The signed unique id differs from the one read in this open: the answers do not come from one chip Do not trust the chip InvalidArgument No trusted key was given Give the verified vendor key FrameError A stored data object has no completion marker, or the value is not the size you expect Do not use the value BufferTooSmall The stored value is longer than 255 bytes and cannot be attested whole (in the model; a chip may answer an error status instead above the 500-byte attested-read limit, A36 ) Attest a shorter object, or read it with Load Bench step (not verified on hardware): attest slot 0 on a dev kit with the vendor attestation key from its certificate (AN12436 Tables 8 and 9, p. 10), then repeat with a wrong trusted key and check AttestationInvalid . Bench step (not verified on hardware): Store values of 255, 300 and 600 bytes on a dev kit and Attest each. 255 bytes must verify; record the error and status word of the other two. The model answers both with the whole value, which the host refuses as BufferTooSmall ; above the 500-byte attested-read limit (AN13030 pp. 248-252) the chip may answer an error status instead ( A36 ). Either way no value is returned.

docs.text: CSR and certificates: get the key certified and keep the chain ¶ The optional se05x::pki layer builds a certification request (PKCS#10, RFC 2986) signed by the key in the chip, stores the certificate your CA issues and the CA certificate as the trust anchor in binary objects, and verifies the chain at boot. See Certificates (PKI) for the whole layer. From a device key to a stored certificate Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Your CA, Factory station, Device firmware and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Device firmware sends generate the device key (inside the chip) to SE05x. Device firmware sends sign the CSR body (ECDSASign) to SE05x. Device firmware sends CSR with the unique id as serialNumber to Factory station. Factory station sends CSR to Your CA. Your CA returns device certificate, CA certificate to Factory station. Factory station sends both certificates to Device firmware. Device firmware sends WriteBinary: certificate and trust anchor (nobody may write them) to SE05x. A note over Device firmware and SE05x says: every boot: read both back, verify the chain. Drawn from: docs/model/csr-flow.seq.yml . /// Step 1: generate the device key inside the chip and read its public half. The policy lets /// anybody sign with it under secure messaging and nobody write, delete or regenerate it. template < AppletGeneration G , PortSet P > Result < pki :: PublicKey > GenerateDeviceKey ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , ObjectId key , std :: span < uint8_t , 65 > public_key ) noexcept { const Result < Policy > policy = PolicyBuilder < G , ObjectClass :: EcKeyPair , Profile :: Strict > {} . ForAllOthers () . template Allow < Rule :: Sign > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Write > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Delete > () . template Forbid < Rule :: Gen > () . RequireSecureMessaging () . Build (); if ( ! policy . ok ()) { return Result < pki :: PublicKey >:: Failure ( policy . error , policy . detail ); } if ( const auto made = device . GenerateEcKey ( key , policy . value , EcCurve :: NistP256 ); ! made . ok ()) { return Result < pki :: PublicKey >:: Failure ( made . error , made . detail ); } return pki :: ReadPublicKey ( device , key , pki :: KeyType :: EcP256 , MutableByteSpan { public_key }); } /// Step 2: a certification request for that key, signed by the chip, with the chip's unique id /// as the subject's serialNumber. The request is checked against its own key before it leaves. template < PortSet P , typename Crypto > Result < std :: size_t > MakeCsr ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , Crypto & crypto , ObjectId key , const pki :: PublicKey & public_key , ByteSpan unique_id , MutableByteSpan csr ) noexcept { constexpr std :: array < uint8_t , 6 > kOrganization { 0x44U , 0x65U , 0x76U , 0x69U , 0x63U , 0x65U }; pki :: Name subject {}; static_cast < void > ( subject . Add ( pki :: Attribute :: Organization , ByteSpan { kOrganization }) . AddHex ( pki :: Attribute :: SerialNumber , unique_id )); const pki :: CsrRequest request { & subject , public_key , nullptr , pki :: key_usage :: kDigitalSignature }; pki :: DeviceSigner < P > signer ( device , key , pki :: KeyType :: EcP256 ); const Result < std :: size_t > built = pki :: BuildCsr ( request , signer , crypto , csr ); if ( ! built . ok ()) { return built ; } pki :: PortVerifier < Crypto > verifier ( crypto ); const auto checked = pki :: VerifyCsr ( ByteSpan { csr }. first ( built . value ), verifier , crypto ); return checked . ok () ? built : Result < std :: size_t >:: Failure ( checked . error , checked . detail ); } /// Step 3: store the certificate the CA issued, and the CA's certificate as the trust anchor, /// each in a new binary object nobody can write; `admin` may delete them to rotate. template < AppletGeneration G , PortSet P > Result < void > ImportCertificates ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , ObjectId certificate , ByteSpan issued , ObjectId anchor , ByteSpan ca_certificate , AuthObject admin ) noexcept { const Result < Policy > policy = pki :: CertificatePolicy < G > ( admin ); if ( ! policy . ok ()) { return Result < void >:: Failure ( policy . error , policy . detail ); } std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > scratch {}; const auto stored_anchor = pki :: StoreCertificate ( device , anchor , ca_certificate , policy . value , scratch ); if ( ! stored_anchor . ok ()) { return stored_anchor ; } return pki :: StoreCertificate ( device , certificate , issued , policy . value , scratch ); } /// At every boot: read the certificate and the anchor back and verify the chain at `now` (Unix /// seconds from a clock you trust). The verified key is the one the chip signs with. template < PortSet P , typename Crypto > Error CheckDeviceCertificate ( se05x :: Device < P >& device , Crypto & crypto , ObjectId certificate , ObjectId anchor , uint64_t now ) noexcept { std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > anchor_bytes {}; std :: array < uint8_t , 1024 > cert_bytes {}; const auto trusted = pki :: LoadTrustAnchor ( device , anchor , anchor_bytes ); const auto cert = pki :: ReadCertificate ( device , certificate , cert_bytes ); if ( ! trusted . ok () || ! cert . ok ()) { return trusted . ok () ? cert . error : trusted . error ; } const std :: array < ByteSpan , 1 > chain { cert . value . der }; const std :: array < pki :: TrustAnchor , 1 > anchors { trusted . value }; pki :: PortVerifier < Crypto > verifier ( crypto ); const pki :: VerifyOptions options { now , pki :: key_usage :: kDigitalSignature , false }; const auto verified = pki :: VerifyChain ( std :: span < const ByteSpan > { chain }, std :: span < const pki :: TrustAnchor > { anchors }, options , verifier , crypto ); return verified . error ; // AttestationInvalid: pki::ReasonOf(verified.detail) says why } What it protects against ¶ Threat Answer A CSR for a key the device does not hold The chip signs the CSR; it is checked against its own key before it leaves A swapped certificate in storage The certificate objects grant write to nobody; the chain is verified at boot against the stored anchor A certificate that is expired or for another key VerifyChain checks the time you give and that the leaf key is the key the chip signs with A certificate is public: anyone may read it, so its integrity is its signature, never its storage. When it fails ¶ Error Meaning What to do InvalidArgument (layer Pki ) Malformed DER, a field outside the profile, no time Fix the input; the reason is in Detail::step AttestationInvalid A signature in the chain does not verify Do not trust the device certificate ObjectExists A certificate is already stored Rotate with the admin authentication object Bench step (not verified on hardware): run the four recipes on a dev kit against a test CA (OpenSSL), then check with openssl verify that the stored chain verifies and that the leaf public key equals GetPublicKey of the slot.

docs.text: Device identity: generate a key and sign ¶ Give each device a NIST P-256 key pair generated inside the chip (WriteECKey with no key bytes, AN12543 p. 80). The private half never exists outside the chip; the device proves who it is by signing (ECDSASign, AN12543 p. 101). Provision a signing key, then sign Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Provision (slot 0) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends CheckObjectExists, WriteECKey (no key bytes, strict policy) to SE05x. A note over SE05x and hrot::Device says: the key pair is generated inside the chip. Firmware sends Sign(key, SHA-256 digest) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDSASign to SE05x. SE05x returns DER signature (R-MAC checked) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns Signature to Firmware. Drawn from: docs/model/sign-call.seq.yml . /// Generate the device key in slot 0 and read its public half. template < PortSet P > Error ProvisionDeviceKey ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , hrot :: EcPublicKey & public_key ) noexcept { constexpr hrot :: Slot kDeviceKey = hrot :: Slot :: At < 0 > (); const std :: array < hrot :: SlotPlan , 1 > plan { hrot :: SlotPlan { kDeviceKey , hrot :: KeyUse :: Sign }}; if ( const auto checked = hrot . CheckPlan ( plan ); ! checked . ok ()) { return checked . error ; // nothing was sent } const auto key = hrot . template Provision < hrot :: KeyUse :: Sign > ( kDeviceKey ); if ( ! key . ok ()) { return key . error ; // ObjectExists: the slot was provisioned before; use Find() } const auto pub = hrot . GetPublicKey ( key . value ); public_key = pub . value ; return pub . error ; } /// Sign a SHA-256 digest with the device key and check the signature on the chip. template < PortSet P > Error SignAndVerify ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , hrot :: Digest digest , hrot :: Signature & out ) noexcept { const auto key = hrot . template Find < hrot :: KeyUse :: Sign > ( hrot :: Slot :: At < 0 > ()); if ( ! key . ok ()) { return key . error ; } const auto signature = hrot . Sign ( key . value , digest ); if ( ! signature . ok ()) { return signature . error ; // PolicyDenied: no secure messaging } out = signature . value ; return hrot . VerifySignature ( key . value , digest , out . View ()). error ; // Ok only when valid } The key's policy allows signing and reading the public half under secure messaging, and forbids write, delete and regeneration for everybody (AN12543 Tables 62 and 63, p. 66). Find<KeyUse::Sign>(slot) gives the key back after a reboot, and only if the slot holds a persistent key pair generated in the chip with the facade's own policy, byte for byte. docs.text: ECDH key agreement and encryption ¶ Agree a shared secret with a peer: the chip combines its private key with the peer's public key and returns the 32-byte x coordinate of the shared point (ECDHGenerateSharedSecret, AN12543 p. 105). Derive a session key from it (HKDF on the host) and encrypt with that key; the private half of the agreement key never leaves the chip. ECDH key agreement Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Peer, Firmware, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Firmware sends Provision (slot 1) (once) to hrot::Device. Peer sends peer public key to Firmware. Firmware sends Agree(key, peer, SecretBuffer) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDHGenerateSharedSecret (encrypted both ways) to SE05x. SE05x returns shared secret (R-ENC, R-MAC) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns SecretBuffer, wiped on failure and at scope end to Firmware. A note over Firmware and hrot::Device says: HKDF, then AES-GCM with the derived key. Drawn from: docs/model/agree-call.seq.yml . /// Agree a secret with a peer. The key lives in slot 1; the secret is wiped when `shared` goes. template < PortSet P > Error AgreeWithPeer ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , const hrot :: EcPublicKey & peer , SecretBuffer < 32 >& shared ) noexcept { auto key = hrot . template Find < hrot :: KeyUse :: Agree > ( hrot :: Slot :: At < 1 > ()); if ( key . error == Error :: ObjectNotFound ) { key = hrot . template Provision < hrot :: KeyUse :: Agree > ( hrot :: Slot :: At < 1 > ()); } if ( ! key . ok ()) { return key . error ; } return hrot . Agree ( key . value , peer , shared ). error ; } What it protects against ¶ Threat Answer Reading the shared secret on the bus The facade sends ECDH only over traffic encrypted both ways ( Full ) An invalid peer point that leaks key bits The facade checks the peer before anything is sent: prefix 04, both coordinates below p, on the P-256 curve; AN12543 4.10.3.1 does not say the chip checks it, so the facade does A secret left in RAM after use SecretBuffer wipes itself; a failed call leaves it empty A chip whose extended features forbid ECDH ( EXTCFG_CRYPTO_EC_FORBID_ECDH , AN12543 Table 9, p. 26) refuses with Unsupported before anything is sent. A key whose policy has POLICY_OBJ_FORBID_DERIVED_OUTPUT (AN12543 Table 63) never returns the secret; the facade's agreement key does not set it, because Agree returns the secret. When it fails ¶ Error Meaning What to do PolicyDenied (layer Hrot ) The traffic is not encrypted both ways Open platform SCP03 at Full InvalidArgument The peer key is not a point on P-256 (prefix, range or curve equation) Reject the peer Unsupported The chip's configuration forbids ECDH Use another variant or configuration FrameError The chip answered a secret of the wrong size The buffer is wiped; retry once, then report Bench step (not verified on hardware): agree with a host key on a dev kit and compare the secret with the one OpenSSL computes from the chip's public key ( GetPublicKey ) and the host private key.

docs.text: Mutual TLS: client credentials in the chip ¶ In mutual TLS the device proves its identity with a client certificate and a signature over the handshake. Keep the client key in the chip as a TlsKey and give your TLS stack a private-key callback that calls TlsSign (ECDSASign over the handshake digest, AN12543 p. 101). The certificate is the one from CSR and certificates . A TLS client signature Figure description and sources Participants, left to right: Server, TLS stack, hrot::Device and SE05x. The steps run from top to bottom. Server sends CertificateRequest to TLS stack. TLS stack sends client certificate (read from the chip's binary object) to Server. TLS stack sends TlsSign(key, handshake digest) to hrot::Device. hrot::Device sends ECDSASign (secure messaging) to SE05x. SE05x returns signature to hrot::Device. hrot::Device returns DER signature to TLS stack. TLS stack sends CertificateVerify to Server. Drawn from: docs/model/tls-sign-call.seq.yml . /// At start-up, once: find the TLS client key (three APDUs), and keep the handle. template < PortSet P > Result < hrot :: TlsKey > FindTlsKey ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot ) noexcept { return hrot . template Find < hrot :: KeyUse :: TlsClient > ( hrot :: Slot :: At < 3 > ()); } /// The private-key callback of a TLS stack: sign the handshake digest with the kept key, one /// APDU per handshake. template < PortSet P > Error TlsSignCallback ( hrot :: Device < P >& hrot , const hrot :: TlsKey & key , hrot :: Digest handshake_digest , hrot :: Signature & out ) noexcept { const auto signature = hrot . TlsSign ( key , handshake_digest ); out = signature . value ; return signature . error ; } Provision the key once with Provision<hrot::KeyUse::TlsClient>(slot) , find it once at start-up (three APDUs) and keep the TlsKey : each handshake then costs one APDU. TlsSign is an ECDSA signature over the digest you give, like Sign . The chip has no separate TLS signing rule, so a TlsClient key has the same policy as a Sign key and the chip would sign any digest with it; what keeps the uses apart is the C++ type ( TlsSign takes only a TlsKey , Sign only a SignKey ) and your slot plan, not the chip. What it protects against ¶ Threat Answer Stealing the client key to impersonate the device The key never leaves the chip Using the TLS key for something else in your code TlsKey is its own type: Sign() with it does not compile. The chip does not enforce this; code that reaches se05x::Device directly can sign anything with it A modified signature on the bus The answer is authenticated by the R-MAC of the channel It does not make the TLS stack itself correct: check the server certificate and the cipher suites in the stack. When it fails ¶ Error Meaning What to do ObjectNotFound from Find The TLS key was not provisioned Provision it in the factory PolicyDenied The answers are not authenticated, or the slot holds another object Open platform SCP03; check the slot plan ThroughputLimited The APDU budget is spent (SE052F, AN13904 p. 28) Reuse TLS sessions; persist the count with SetWindowCount Bench step (not verified on hardware): connect a dev kit to an OpenSSL test server with openssl s_server -Verify 1 and the CA of the client certificate; the handshake must complete and the server log must show the device certificate.
